items.title: Sinuiju flooding stalls North Korea-China cargo trade for days
items.summary: Heavy rain in Sinuiju has disrupted cross-border cargo truck traffic between North Korea and China, further cooling Chinese investment sentiment that had been building around the anticipated opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, a China-funded crossing linking Sinuiju and Dandong that has stood largely unused since its completion in 2014. Cargo trucks traveling between […]
items.body_text:
Heavy rain in Sinuiju has disrupted cross-border cargo truck traffic between North Korea and China, further cooling Chinese investment sentiment that had been building around the anticipated opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, a China-funded crossing linking Sinuiju and Dandong that has stood largely unused since its completion in 2014.
Cargo trucks traveling between Dandong in China’s Liaoning province and Sinuiju in North Korea’s North Pyongan province stopped running for more than two days starting Aug. 24, a source in North Korea told Daily NK on Friday.
“Trucks that had entered North Korea before Aug. 24 could not return to China, and new trucks could not enter either,” the source said. “There is talk that the cause was a problem in Sinuiju with processing, transporting or storing cargo.”
The exact cause of the suspension has not been officially confirmed, but Chinese trading circles believe it is likely directly linked to recent flooding in Sinuiju caused by heavy rain.
Daily NK previously reported that heavy rain in Sinuiju overwhelmed the city’s weak drainage system, flooding low-lying areas and cutting off electricity and water supplies in some neighborhoods.
Local observers say the low-lying Apkang and Yokjon neighborhoods, which sit near the North Korea-China trade route, may also have seen roads and buildings flooded. Trade and vehicle traffic were likely halted temporarily to prevent further damage during the unloading, storage and transport of cargo, according to the assessment.
Investment mood turns cold
Notably, the incident is also weighing on investment sentiment toward Sinuiju, which had been rising in recent months.
“Businesspeople already knew Sinuiju was geographically vulnerable to flooding, but repeated flood damage like this inevitably changes their thinking,” the source said. “Just as things seemed to be going well, the uncontrollable variable of natural disaster resurfaced and threw cold water on the investment mood.”
The source added, “Many people had shown interest in the idea of developing the surrounding area into an international economic zone once the New Yalu River Bridge opens. But after this incident, there is a growing sense that there are problems that need to be resolved before questions like when the bridge will open or where to invest.”
Among Chinese businesspeople, a growing view holds that simply signing contracts with North Korea and building factories or warehouses is not enough to guarantee stability, and that North Korea must first upgrade its infrastructure to withstand flooding.
“There is growing concern that without protective construction work, such as raising the ground level with soil or rock fill and installing proper waterproofing and drainage systems, a single heavy rain could cause serious damage,” the source said. “Businesspeople have also grown more alert to natural disasters after seeing a string of sudden flood damage in border regions, including recent flooding in Nepal.”
The repeated flooding in Sinuiju is once again highlighting the city’s geographic limitations and weak infrastructure. As flood risk emerges as a major variable for Chinese businesspeople who had shown interest in investing in North Korea, attention is turning to what impact this will have on development around the New Yalu River Bridge, an area that had drawn attention amid expanding North Korea-China customs trade.
Reporting from inside North Korea
Daily NK operates networks of sources inside North Korea who document events in real-time and transmit information through secure channels. Unlike reporting based on state media, satellite imagery, or defector accounts from years past, our journalism comes directly from people currently living under the regime. We verify reports through multiple independent sources and cross-reference details before publication.
Our sources remain anonymous because contact with foreign media is treated as a capital offense in North Korea — discovery means imprisonmen

items.title: North Korea’s Sinuiju underwater again as drainage system fails
items.summary: Sinuiju, the North Pyongan province city that suffered catastrophic flood damage in the summer of 2024, is underwater again, this time because a short burst of intense rain overwhelmed the city’s weak drainage system rather than the Yalu River overflowing its banks. With low-lying neighborhoods submerged and power and water cut off, the flooding has […]
items.body_text:
Sinuiju, the North Pyongan province city that suffered catastrophic flood damage in the summer of 2024, is underwater again, this time because a short burst of intense rain overwhelmed the city’s weak drainage system rather than the Yalu River overflowing its banks. With low-lying neighborhoods submerged and power and water cut off, the flooding has become the latest sign of how fragile North Korea’s urban infrastructure remains against extreme weather.
According to a Daily NK source in North Pyongan province who spoke Thursday, heavy rain pounded the Sinuiju area on Aug. 23 and 24. The downpour briefly let up on Aug. 25 before picking up again overnight into Aug. 26.
“During the flooding in 2024, the river overflowed and that caused the damage. This time, the damage happened because the rainwater couldn’t drain away,” the source said. “The standing water can’t recede, and since it keeps raining, there’s even less chance for it to drain, so many areas remain flooded.”
“The rain stopped briefly on Aug. 25, and we thought the water might start receding, but it began raining again overnight into the early hours of Aug. 26,” the source added. “With the rain continuing like this, people don’t know when the water will finally recede, and they’re feeling anxious.”
The pattern of this flooding is markedly different from the 2024 disaster, according to the source. In 2024, the Yalu River overflowed and heavily damaged Wihwa Island and areas along the riverbank. This time, weak drainage conditions caused flooding across low-lying areas throughout the city.
In Sumun neighborhood, both electricity and water service remained cut off as of Aug. 26, and a significant number of single-story homes were submerged, forcing people to evacuate to higher ground. Temporary shelters have also been set up in some neighborhoods, including Ryonsang and Ryonha, to house flood victims as part of the response, according to the source.
Little state aid expected this time
Amid the damage, flood victims are reportedly resigned to the idea that nationwide recovery assistance will not follow this time, meaning they will have to rebuild their homes and belongings on their own once the water recedes.
“During the previous flooding, the Yalu River overflowed and the damage was highly visible from the outside, and the Marshal (Kim Jong Un) personally visited the area, so nationwide recovery assistance followed. This time, though, the visible damage isn’t as extensive,” the source said. “So there’s a strong sense among people that they shouldn’t expect much state support and will need to rebuild on their own.”
“In terms of the actual damage people have suffered, this time isn’t much different from before,” the source added. “With electricity and water cut off and homes and belongings submerged for days, people are struggling not only with immediate concerns like food and shelter, but even more with the uncertainty of how they’ll rebuild their lives once the water finally recedes.”
The latest flooding is seen as a case that exposes both the topographical characteristics of the Sinuiju area and its vulnerable drainage infrastructure. With North Korean authorities not disclosing detailed information about the damage this time, attention is turning to how extensive and thorough any future recovery efforts will be.
Rodong Sinmun reported Aug. 26 that rain and showers fell across most of the country between Aug. 23 and 24 due to a low-pressure trough and the seasonal rain front, with heavy rain also reported in several areas of North Pyongan province, some areas of South Pyongan province, and localized areas of Jagang province.
According to the newspaper, on Aug. 24 alone, Kusong received 408 millimeters of rain, Sinuiju 379 millimeters, Chonma 365 millimeters, Wihwa Island 329 millimeters, Uiju and Taechon 319 millimeters, Phihyon 267 millimeters, Nyongbyon 224 millimeters and Taegwan 216 millimeters, all considered extremely heavy rainfall. items.title: A viral Facebook call-out for ring-ins saved this country footy side
items.summary: Violet Town opened its club to players from far and wide, building the ultimate "ressies" battler team to compete in the Kyabram District Football Netball League.
items.body_text:
Violet Town was struggling to fill its reserves footy team until a viral Facebook post
There are more conventional ways to fill a football side, but for a country club struggling for senior numbers, posting a call-out for ring-ins on Facebook may have saved its season.
Violet Town Football Netball Club is located two hours north-east of Melbourne. The town of around 1,000 people is most famous for its community market, birthing the band Killing Heidi and for streets named after flowers.
But at 2 Tulip Street, the address of Violet Town Recreation Reserve, there was concern for its reserves team after forfeiting round one.
The coach of the seconds, Ryan Lloyd-Williams, took the unusual step of posting on social media in a desperate attempt for numbers.
There was no offer of payment or petrol money, just a chance to pull on a jumper at a reserves side being beaten by 100 points each week in the Kyabram District Football Netball League.
The Victorian Metro & Country Football Recruiting Page on Facebook is littered with clubs looking for players and players looking for a game.
Each post might receive a handful of likes, but Lloyd-Williams's post went gangbusters.
It received more than 300 likes and comments combined, and Lloyd-Williams said without this response it was likely season over for the Violet Town twos.
"In October last year numbers were looking good and I was quite chuffed," he said.
"We got to the start of the year and they dwindled off, and it got to round one and we had about eight to pick from. So I did this post on this group.
"I thought if we get one or two it's worth it but it blew up. I think it had a couple of hundred likes in a couple of days. I think the next game was three days later and we got eight from that post.
"They brought friends, so I reckon in and out we've had fourteen or fifteen players from it and quite a few of them have played seniors as well.
"We've had to forfeit one other game, but I reckon we would have had to can the year straight away if that [Facebook post] didn't happen."
One family from Bendigo provided three brothers, a father-in-law and even a grandfather, while others have travelled from Kinglake, Melbourne and Shepparton.
"They're spread from everywhere. None of them knew anyone so on the first day it was interesting," Lloyd-Williams said.
"I met eight new blokes, they all met new blokes, there were a lot of handshakes."
One of those recruits, aptly named Bailey Smith, is still in high school, but he and his father Brad travelled from Melbourne to play because, according to Smith, "Dad's cousin is married to the ressies team manager."
It is a valid enough reason to pull on the Towners jumper.
Violet Town co-president Lachlan McKinnon said this approach to finding players created a buzz in the community.
"It got a lot of chatter, a lot of comments around locally, and other teams [saying] 'what are you doing that for?'" he said.
"Well, we're needing numbers and it's better to field a team, even if you get kind of flogged, than to not have a team.
"So we put them in a jumper and send them out. A lot of them — I'm not sure how much football they've ever played.
"If I'm really honest it's a bit random. I look around and think 'my god I've never seen you in my life'.
"My happiest day at the club is when [the club room] is packed after the game and everyone is having a good time.
"A lot of these guys don't hang around as much and that's okay. You can't force them to. It's one of the things we try to drive in our senior program — we want you involved in the club."
From ring-in to acting captain
Lachlan Munn is an example of the player McKinnon would like to fill the Towners' senior sides with.
Munn said Lloyd-Williams's plea came up as a suggested post in his feed and he decided to get in touch, playing footy for the first time since under-17s in 2018.
He lives a 45-minute drive away in Mooroopna, so is committed to attending training and games, and plans on sticking around next season.

items.title: Season over for Kangaroos AFLW star after spinal fusion surgery
items.summary: AFLW premiership midfielder Mia King of the Kangaroos undergoes season-ending spinal fusion surgery after feeling neck pain after a match in Brisbane.
items.body_text:
Mia King remains in Queensland after successful surgery to fuse the C5 and C6 vertebrae in her neck.
King, part of the Kangaroos' 2024 premiership win, felt neck pain after her team's win over Brisbane last weekend.
North Melbourne's club doctor says King is not expected to miss next season.
Two-time AFLW premiers North Melbourne have lost midfielder Mia King for the season after she required spinal fusion surgery for a neck injury.
The premiership midfielder reported neck pain following North's win over Brisbane Lions last weekend.
King underwent a thorough medical examination in Brisbane, which revealed a disc injury near her spinal cord.
She remains in Queensland recovering after having successful surgery to fuse together the C5 and C6 vertebrae in her neck.
The Kangaroos confirmed the procedure would sideline King for the rest of the 2026 season.
"We will continue monitoring Mia in her recovery but we don't expect this type of surgery to stop her from returning to play in 2027," club doctor Victoria Norbury said in a statement.
King was part of North Melbourne's premiership-winning team in 2024, but she missed out on last year's grand final win after an ongoing PCL knee injury.
The Kangaroos are again at the top of the ladder after two rounds this season, with the best percentage in the AFLW.
North Melbourne general manager of women's football Erin Lorenzini said the club would support King as she began her recovery.
"We wrap our arms around Mia," Lorenzini said. "We are devastated for her, but also full of admiration for how incredibly strong she has been this week.
"As a proud Jawoyn woman, she was particularly looking forward to wearing our Indigenous Round jumper in Launceston this weekend.
"We have a very close group of players and staff, and all our thoughts will be with her as we run out against the Bulldogs on Saturday."

items.title: More than a bridge: Remembering Brisbane’s 2001 Goodwill Games
items.summary: It cost $30 million and left only a footbridge, but the 2001 Goodwill Games – 25 years ago today – permanently altered Brisbane’s global footprint.
items.body_text:
More than a bridge: Remembering Brisbane’s 2001 Goodwill Games
It cost $30 million and left only a footbridge, but the 2001 Goodwill Games – 25 years ago today – permanently altered Brisbane’s global footprint.
A stepping stone, or second-rate sideshow. The Brisbane 2001 Goodwill Games could be remembered in several ways, perhaps none as enduring as the pedestrian bridge that bears its name.
Friday marked a quarter-century since of the Goodwill Games opening ceremony at the Brisbane Entertainment Centre, with competition starting 25 years ago on Saturday.
Created by recently departed media mogul Ted Turner in 1986 after the Cold War-era Moscow 1980 and Los Angeles 1984 Olympic boycotts, the Goodwill Games were designed to bring elite athletes from rival nations together and promote international goodwill.
Unlike other competitions, the event offered substantial prize money – about $US10 million by the time Brisbane came around – and sought to provide a politically neutral stage.
The Queensland government spent $30 million in 1997 to attract the Goodwill Games, beating Shanghai, Guangzhou, Hong Kong, Cape Town, Osaka, Rio de Janeiro and Buenos Aires.
Brisbane would become the first, and ultimately the last, host outside the United States and Russia.
Then-premier Peter Beattie says it was part of a broader strategy to elevate Brisbane’s international profile.
“For us, it was a step-stone of using sport to attract major events to Queensland,” he says.
“We had a major event strategy designed to not just attract the world’s attention, but to put Brisbane on the world map.”
Quite literally, as 2001 Goodwill Games chief executive Campbell Rose recalls.
“It seems a bit trivial, but the fact was that Brisbane didn’t exist on the CNN weather map. Melbourne did, Sydney did, but Brisbane didn’t,” he says.
“Well, since the Goodwill Games, Brisbane’s been on the CNN weather map.”
Having the network’s owner behind the Games helped, but Beattie says Turner’s involvement meant far more than map placement.
“Ted Turner was a billionaire. Obviously, business people came with him and we were looking to get money invested into Queensland,” he says.
“Australia’s problem is that we are short of cash. We don’t have a lot of capital, so you’ve got to find imaginative ways to attract people to come.”
The Goodwill Games attracted potential investors from the world’s largest markets. The USA. China. Japan. Germany. And of course, Russia.
As Rose says: “It projected Brisbane right into those markets with pinpoint accuracy.”
Held less than a year after Sydney 2000, Australia was basking in the post-Olympic glow when Turner’s circus rolled into town.
Rose, a Melburnian who was poached from the city’s major events office, says Sydney 2000’s shadow loomed large, and the Goodwill Games attracted its share of sceptics.
“You would get things like, ‘Is it a second-rate event for a second-rate city?’” he says.
“There was that cloud of Sydney being a hard act to follow and, yes, it was a hard act to follow, but we did a couple of key things.
“We developed an outstanding cultural festival called Paint the Town Red. We lit the Story Bridge and staged events across the city throughout the Games, which really resonated with the Brisbane population.
“The other key thing we did, very successfully, was that the Goodwill Games was all about having the best 10 or so athletes in every discipline compete.”
Investment, tourism and putting-on-the-map aside, the Goodwill Games were an elite sporting competition and that invitation-only format set them apart from the Olympics.
No qualifiers, no Eric the Eels.
Instead, there was Ian Thorpe. Michael Johnson. The since-disgraced Marion Jones.
And two-time Sydney 2000 Olympic gold medallist Grant Hackett.

items.title: After the parades and plaudits: How the tide turned for ‘steel saviour’ Sanjeev Gupta
items.summary: The billionaire was given a hero’s welcome for saving Whyalla and the planet – but all was not what it seemed.
items.body_text:
After the parades and plaudits: How the tide turned for ‘steel saviour’ Sanjeev Gupta
The billionaire was given a hero’s welcome for saving Whyalla and the planet – but all was not what it seemed.
Sanjeev Gupta is a puzzle. He is certainly a world-class salesman. On that let’s all agree. It is how he managed to borrow so much money, how he came to be a billionaire and how he persuaded so many decent people to share his vision.
But surprisingly, the silver-tongued steel tycoon is no brash fairground spruiker. He is a shy man, an introvert: quiet and softly spoken. Picture a besuited Dr Evil in the Austin Powers comedy movies and you’ll get a fair idea of what he looks like. Although Gupta, of course, was promising to save the world and not destroy it.
Naturally, he loved money and expensive toys. But those who observed him from up close believed he was driven by a craving for attention and the thrill of the deal. He was an outsider who wanted to be on the inside and be accepted into the Establishment.
The people who liked him said he was smart, generous, likeable, loyal and sincere. Some even called him a visionary. But many saw a less attractive side. One former executive described him to me as “the most selfish man I’ve ever met”. A second who knew him well branded him a narcissist. A third said he wouldn’t believe anything that came out of his mouth. Yet all agreed he had world-class charm, if he chose to turn it on.
So what do we know of his formative years? Before the luxury homes in London, Sydney and Dubai? Before the private plane and helicopter, a yacht in every port and a slew of offshore companies and trusts to keep his baubles safe? Before he was hailed as the “Saviour of Steel” for rescuing South Australia’s famous Whyalla steelworks. Before all of it – the worldwide business empire built on billions of dollars of Other People’s Money, and the disaster waiting to happen north of Adelaide?
Sanjeev Gupta was born in India in 1971 and spent his childhood in the Punjab, in the industrial city of Ludhiana, often known as the Manchester of India. His father, Parduman (“PK”) Gupta, was a self-made man who left school at 11 and started out selling nuts and bolts before making his fortune manufacturing Victor bicycles in India and trading commodities in Nigeria.
Gupta was the third of four children, who, according to his big sister Anjali, was always trying to prove himself. “You know, he sometimes needed more attention,” she told the BBC in 2016, “but he was very driven, very ambitious … He was a very quiet child, and he wouldn’t want to talk to people.”
On Anjali’s account, Gupta was wilful and determined. At the age of 11, he convinced his seven-year-old brother to run away from their exclusive boarding school at Shimla in the Himalayas, which they hated, and catch a bus back home, six hours away. “They gave us a shock of our life because they had to check into a hotel overnight,” his sister recalled.
Four years later, as Sanjeev was turning 15, he persuaded his father to send him to one of England’s most expensive boarding schools, St Edmund’s Canterbury, where his elder brother Raj was already a student. Coming into fifth form when most of his classmates had already chosen their friends, he was younger than most and was small, chubby, quiet and shy.
“He wasn’t bullied but he was certainly teased,” says one old schoolmate, who is now a successful businessman. “He had a bit of an accent. One boy called him De Gupita Singh and would chant the name at him, laughing.”
At the start, Gupta was homesick and missed his mum and dad. He slept in a big, cold, chapel-like dorm with 50 other boys, one of whom recalls the 15-year-old crying in his sleep. And while life at St Edmund’s wasn’t quite as brutal as Rugby School in that famous Victorian novel, Tom Brown’s Schooldays, it was certainly a tougher environment than would be tolerated today. items.body_text:
The families of an Australian defence force member and two Sydney boys who went missing with their parents in Nepal remain hopeful they will be found safe.
Dozens of Australians are missing after devastating flooding on the Nepal-Tibet border. Nepal’s disaster management authority said on Friday that the total number of people missing had risen sharply to more than 1,900 swelled by 933 workers on hydropower projects on the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers where a wall of water powered down on Wednesday morning. The number of people killed is at least 584.
One Australian woman contacted her family on Friday morning to tell them that she had survived the flood, the first of those reported missing to be confirmed safe.
Among the missing Australians is Karan Bhardwaj, a 40-year-old Brisbane-based member of the Royal Australian air force who was travelling in Nepal with Kailash Journeys.
“Karan is a dad to my beautiful seven-year-old nephew, as well as a brother, uncle and brother in law,” said his family member Jen, who did not want her surname published.
“He is so desperately loved by his family and right now we are desperately praying, hoping and believing that Karan is safe, alive and somehow making his way back to us.”
Shylaja Muralitharan, 42, her husband, Chandrasekaran Muralitharan, 47, and their two sons Ashwin, 14, and Aarush, 11, were taking part in a pilgrimage when the flood hit on Wednesday.
Shylaja’s younger sister, Vaishnavi, said that she had lost contact with the family shortly after breakfast on the morning of the flood.
The family of four planned to head towards an immigration checkpoint on the Tibet-Nepal border soon after, as part of the group of 15 Australians trekking with the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour.
“Just like everyone else that’s part of that group, we’re really worried, but hopeful,” Vaishnavi said.
“Hopeful that they’re safe and just waiting to be rescued.
“It’s a very difficult time for our whole family … I just want to make people aware that they’re there, and we’re waiting, and we just want them to return.”
Vaishnavi, who asked that her surname not be published, confirmed the family were close with other members of the group who had also travelled from Sydney for the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet.
The family had been training together for the long walk, she said.
“They had been planning for some time, and preparing, because it’s quite a trek.
“They were all working very hard together to make sure they could successfully complete it.
“We just didn’t expect anything like this.”
Vaishnavi said it was difficult to get clear information about what was being done to find those missing. She has spoken with Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade officials.
“We do want to know what efforts are being made … we’re not aware of what is actually happening there.”
Australian woman Sumi Adhikari was at an immigration office at the Gyirong Post crossing when the flood waters hit. She was travelling with an Isha Foundation pilgrimage to the region.
Her husband, Nava Pandey, has travelled to Nepal and is desperately seeking information about her whereabouts.
“She was in the same area when the flood happened,” said a flyer produced by Adhikari’s family, and published with their permission. “If anyone has seen her or has any information about her, please contact the family immediately.”
Bharat Mangwani, 42, was travelling with the Isha Foundation as part of a pilgrimage to Lake Manasarovar when his family lost contact with him on Wednesday morning.
He was last seen at Gyirong before the group was set to depart for Kathmandu and then Delhi, his close friend Kushagra Tiwari said.
Mangwani’s family, including his nine-year-old son and three-year-old daughter, have travelled to India with a family friend, while his wife has gone on to Kathmandu to look for any information.
“All of us are praying for him and hopefully he comes back to us soon,” Tiwari said.

items.body_text:
Australia’s Nepali community plan to host vigils to remember the victims of the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster to coincide with a day of mourning, as the number of people killed continues to rise.
As Australia’s Nepali diaspora wait for the full scale of the disaster to become clear, community members are desperately waiting to hear from missing relatives and friends.
 Nepali authorities said on Friday that the death toll had risen to 579, with the number missing rising sharply to more than 1,900, after massive flash floods and landslides tore through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river basins on Wednesday.
The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, on Friday morning confirmed the number of Australians missing in the floods had increased to 39 as she unveiled a $5m support package.
Wong told the ABC that Australians who wished to donate could do so via the Emergency Action Alliance website – run by a group of Australian charities and humanitarian organisations.
Nepali Australians gathered for candlelight prayers on Thursday night and held a minute’s silence for those lost to the floods.
Dr Tilak Pokhrel, president of the Australian Nepalese Multicultural Centre (ANMC), said community organisations in Victoria would host a vigil when the Nepali government announced an upcoming national day of mourning.
“Community members just want to say we are with you for those who are affected,” he said.
“We want to have an event where we all can gather and show our solidarity to support them.
“Let’s work together, let’s pray together, and let’s go through this pain together.”
Pokhrel said the centre would extend its opening hours for the next few days so faith leaders could provide support.
“People are waiting for the news. They are checking the news every hour,” he said.
Chudamani Sapkota, the general secretary of Non-Resident Nepali Association, said its New South Wales branch would host a candlelight vigil on Saturday evening in Sydney.
“This is devastating news for all the Nepalese diaspora,” he said.
Sapkota said the organisation was trying to support Nepali Australians seeking to locate their missing relatives.
“There’s no network, nothing at the moment,” he said. “This is a very tough time.”
Melbourne student Rakshya Pandey’s family home and two grocery shops in the Nuwakot district, hit by the flash flooding, have been destroyed. Her father, who was injured after being struck by an object in the flooding, is receiving treatment in a Kathmandu hospital.
“Whenever I see the detail of the people missing or the flood or everything, it’s just so scary, and I’m scared … I can’t do anything. I feel so helpless,” she said.
Pandey fears there will be future flooding in Nepal.
Ashok Bahadur Dhungel, who lives in Canberra, has been trying to reach his nephew who works for the Upper Trishuli hydropower plant, which sat on one of the Nepali rivers that flooded. He said his nephew has not been online for two days.
“We hope he is still alive,” he said.
Dhungel heard through friends that his mother, who lives in the Nuwakot district, had survived. But he has been unable to speak to her due to power outages.
“She is everything to me,” he said.
Tenzin Khangsar, co-chair of the Australia Tibet Council, said the Tibetan community was “shocked and devastated” about the flooding. He said prayer events would be planned to commemorate the victims.
Diaspora community organisations are also crowdfunding for the Nepali government’s disaster relief fund.
Chiran Tiwari, president of the Nepalese Welfare Society based in Sydney, said the organisation had created a GoFundMe page to raise money for the Nepali prime minister’s natural disaster relief fund.
Tiwari said one of the welfare society’s executive member’s relatives was missing in Nepal, with the community rallying around to provide support to them.
“The situation is very sad for the community,” he said. “Everyone’s eyes is tearing so the situation is very difficult.”

items.title: Iran war hits 6-month milestone with Trump's attention largely elsewhere
items.summary: A number of U.S. lawmakers called on Donald Trump to end the war with Iran as it reached its six-month mark on Friday, while the U.S. president has given off mixed signals regarding the state of the conflict.
items.body_text:
Iran war hits 6-month milestone with Trump's attention largely elsewhere
Trump posts 'mission accomplished,' administration focuses on Iran's economic troubles
A number of U.S. lawmakers called on Donald Trump to end the war with Iran as it reached its six-month mark on Friday, while the U.S. president has given off mixed signals regarding the state of the conflict.
Trump has said that the combined effects of the military's offensive strikes and blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have helped the U.S. achieve its objectives. On social media on Wednesday, he shared a post declaring "MISSION ACCOMPLISHED 2026," alongside AI-generated images that included the face of Iranian supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed on Feb. 28 as the U.S. and Israel launched airstrikes to begin the war.
Tehran and Washington have exchanged little more than bellicose statements in recent weeks, leaving the diplomacy to third parties, and Trump has been more preoccupied this week, at least publicly, with his anger over Canada calling a halt to trade talks on tariffs.
It is expected that the U.S. president will increasingly turn his attention to the Nov. 3 midterms, where he has been engaged in efforts to influence how votes are cast, while preparing for a unique, midterm Republican mini-convention in two weeks' time.
Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives' armed service committees, released a statement Friday raising a number of outstanding issues the war has caused, but leading with the toll to those serving in the military.
"Losses continue to accumulate, including 19 American service members killed and over 750 wounded, while thousands of innocent civilians have been killed across the region," said Smith. "Tens of billions of dollars of taxpayers’ money is being wasted while driving up the cost of gas, utilities, and groceries at home and throttling economies around the world."
'More costly and more unstable'
The U.S. and Israel have killed a number of Iran's top religious, military and political officials and Khamenei's successor, his son Mojtaba, hasn't been seen in public amid reports he was seriously injured early in the war.
As well, it has been estimated that the price of rice is up some 60 per cent since the war began and beef 150 per cent higher for Iranians, who have also dealt with long lines to fill up vehicles. The International Monetary Fund forecasts that Iran's gross domestic product will contract more than 5 per cent this year.
But costs have also been incurred on the U.S. side beyond the literal price tag for Operation Epic Fury, from the approval rating for Trump multiple polls to higher prices at gas pumps for many Americans due to the disruption in oil markets. The war has also strained relations between the White House and allies in Europe, the Middle East and Asia, as Trump has expressed anger that they haven't supported the U.S. in the war.
- Trump orders joint military exercises with South Korea to be scaled back
- Trump threatens to bomb Oman if it 'gets in the way' with Iran
Trump "has made the world more costly and more unstable," Brett Bruen, a former U.S. diplomat now at the D.C.-area public affairs agency Global Situation Room, told CBC News on Friday.
Iran found leverage after the initial shock and awe of the U.S. strikes through its own drone attacks and mining in the critical Strait of Hormuz. That dissuaded commercial vessels from countries not friendly to the regime from transiting the passage where substantial amounts of oil and liquefied natural gas typically were moved.
The U.S. eventually responded with its own naval blockade to prevent the movement of ships to Iranian ports. Trump has repeatedly said the strait is open, including this week, but ship-tracking services have estimated activity at roughly 5 per cent to 15 per cent of pre-war volumes.
Democrats earlier this week called for more transparency on the cost of the war. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth

items.title: What the CIA director’s mystery trip to Moscow says about Putin's next move
items.summary: An unannounced but highly visible flight to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe aboard a U.S. Air Force transport plane this week has ignited a fierce debate over Vladimir Putin’s next military move. With Russia’s volunteer recruitment drying up and its economy straining under the weight of 1.4 million casualties, intelligence briefs suggest Putin is preparing a massive, unpopular mobilization of 600,000 new troops.
items.body_text:
What the CIA director’s mystery trip to Moscow says about Putin's next move
Russia's president appears poised to escalate conflict in Eastern Europe
As Russia’s war against Ukraine reaches an inflection point, a conspicuous U.S. intelligence mission to Moscow this week has revealed a fractured debate among allies over Vladimir Putin’s next move.
For weeks now, analysts have speculated that Russia’s strongman president has given up on the notion that U.S. President Donald Trump might be able to coerce Ukraine into meeting his maximalist surrender terms. The thinking is Putin may have decided his five-year war against the country can only be concluded by expanding the conflict.
With Russia’s economy worsening and the pool of volunteers willing to accept a generous paycheque to fight in Ukraine dwindling, Putin could be facing several options.
Ukrainian intelligence officials believe he will soon initiate an unpopular mass mobilization that could send hundreds of thousands of new conscripts into battle, with the goal of overwhelming Ukraine's overstretched defences.
Soldiers from Russia’s poorer regions have made up a disproportionate amount of the fighting force in Ukraine. A country-wide mobilization could draw in men from the more affluent major cities.
Military think-tanks on both sides of the Atlantic have also warned Putin could try to divide Ukraine’s backers in NATO by staging some kind of provocation in Eastern Europe aimed at splitting the alliance.
Presumed and confirmed Russia hybrid attacks across Europe — including attempted assassinations, sabotage and frequent drone incursions — have all intensified of late. But planners remain concerned that Russia could be tempted to seize a slice of Russian-speaking territory in a neighbouring country as a test to see how the alliance would respond.
Russian officials themselves have raised the possibility this week that they could strike directly at Western weapons manufacturers who supply Ukraine, most notably in Great Britain.
Mystery visit
The speculation over Putin’s next move hit a fever pitch earlier this week after the unusual visit by CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Russia.
Rather than slipping into Moscow on a business jet, the standard protocol for clandestine diplomacy, Ratcliffe arrived at Vnukovo airport aboard a massive, highly visible U.S. Air Force C-17 Globemaster.
Its transponder broadcast the flight path openly across the Atlantic.
U.S. officials appeared to want the world to know Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow was significant and that they had something they wanted the Russians to hear clearly.
"It kind of reached a point inside the administration where they said, ‘We need to read the Russians the riot act,'" said Glen Howard with the Saratoga Foundation, a Washington, D.C.-based security think-tank with a focus on Ukraine.
But what message was Ratcliffe trying to convey?
Initially, the Wall Street Journal reported the mission was a direct ultimatum to Putin: Back off an escalating grey-zone campaign of hybrid sabotage against NATO's eastern flank or risk triggering a direct allied response.
Military planners have long contemplated whether Putin, in order to get a favourable settlement in Ukraine, might try to draw the United States or NATO directly into the war. Staging a modest attack on a small Baltic nation and testing the Article 5 collective defence provision of the NATO treaty might be one way to do that.
The following day, however, Trump himself appeared to dismiss this, saying he wasn’t worried about a Russian attack on NATO, calling Radcliffe’s trip "semi-routine."
Hours later, the New York Times published an account along the lines of what Trump said that contradicted the earlier reporting. It suggested NATO was not the main topic of the meeting; instead, the warning was for Putin to end his war on Ukraine before Russia’s economic and military situation worsened.
Canada at the front
Canada’s largest overseas military deployment is in the Baltics. More

items.title: U.S. may seek win with Mexico in wake of collapsed trade talks with Canada, says ex-negotiator
items.summary: The collapse of trade talks between Ottawa and Washington could see U.S. negotiators try to "aggressively" secure a win with Mexico in their ongoing bilateral talks, says a former Mexican trade negotiator.
items.body_text:
U.S. may seek win with Mexico in wake of collapsed trade talks with Canada, says ex-negotiator
Meanwhile, Mexico's secretary of economy says it's in everyone's interest to find common ground
The collapse of trade talks between Ottawa and Washington could see U.S. negotiators try to "aggressively" secure a win with Mexico in their ongoing bilateral talks, says a former Mexican trade negotiator.
Kenneth Smith Ramos, Mexico's former chief technical negotiator during the initial 2017 to 2019 Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) negotiations, says he expects the U.S. to try to fashion a framework agreement with Mexico before the end of the year, pushing resolutions around thornier matters into 2027 — like the U.S. seeking to put restrictions around Mexican agricultural exports.
"It is a possibility that in the upcoming [negotiating] rounds, weeks or months … that the U.S., for political reasons, like it did with the European Union … comes out and says, 'we have a framework agreement,'" said Smith Ramos, a partner with Mexico City-based Agon, a corporate consulting and legal services firm, in an interview with CBC News.
"I see that as a probability."
- ExclusiveTrump's top trade negotiator disputes Canadian assertion that U.S. made last-minute demands
- Canada, U.S. far apart on tariff deal as deadline looms: sources
Canada and Mexico have both been engaging with the U.S. individually to settle tariff and other specific bilateral trade irritants in hopes of firming up agreements before entering into trilateral talks on amending and extending CUSMA.
Talks between Canada and the U.S. fell apart on Aug. 21 when Prime Minister Mark Carney pulled his negotiators back to Ottawa. Carney said the U.S. introduced last minute demands on culture, autos and sovereignty that Canada could not stomach.
The talks were aimed at forestalling a U.S. threat to impose 50 per cent tariffs on a wide range of Canadian products, impacting about $27-billion worth of Canadian goods.
Canada has since retaliated with dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs on more than 700 different U.S. imports that come into force on Sept. 8.
The Canada-U.S. trade dispute has now indefinitely delayed any trilateral talks on advancing CUSMA, said Smith Ramos.
"We don't know what is going to happen with these tariffs and threats."
The U.S. announced on July 1 that it would not extend the CUSMA agreement in favour of renegotiating the terms of the deal.
Canada and Mexico both wanted to extend the agreement. The two countries are adamant the continental trade agreement is good for all three countries.
Mexico's Secretary of Economy Marcelo Ebrard told reporters Thursday that tensions between Canada and the U.S. don't "favour" Mexico and that it's in everyone's interest to find common ground and move forward.
"Hopefully they will come to some agreement, they were very close just a few days ago," said Ebrard, who is heading to Washington, D.C., next month for another round of bilateral talks.
"The North American region needs to integrate, we need to work together one way or another, and we expect it to happen, but it's difficult to know when."
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum also chose her words carefully when asked about Canada-U.S. trade tensions earlier this week. Sheinbaum spoke with Carney on Aug. 20, the day before the prime minister pulled the plug on trade talks.
"I spoke with Prime Minister Carney on Thursday. I believe that this breakdown hadn't happened yet. I don't want to call it a breakdown, this disagreement — it's better said that way, this disagreement in talks," said Sheinbaum, during her Monday morning news conference.
The Sheinbaum administration has to handle the matter delicately while managing their own unresolved issues at the trade talk table with the U.S., according to Solange Marquez, vice-president of policy with the Canadian Council for the Americas.

items.title: Consequences of six months of war in Iran include Trump paying a political price, hit to global economy
items.summary: Iran has not surrendered, shipping through Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted, and there is no clear path to ending the conflict
items.body_text:
Six months after the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran, the war that President Donald Trump has called a “little excursion” has become a deeply unpopular stalemate that threatens to derail his presidency.
Iran has not surrendered, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted, and there is no clear path to ending the conflict that Trump once predicted would be over in four weeks.
Now, in apparent recognition that further military strikes won’t force concessions from Iran, the U.S. is reverting to a campaign of economic pressure in hopes of further weakening Iran’s government. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has told allies it’s unlikely the U.S. will launch new attacks “for the time being.”
What happens next is unclear but many of the war’s probable enduring consequences – for the United States, Iran and the global economy – are already apparent.
Here are six of those:
1. Trump is paying a political price
The war was unpopular at the outset and has become more so. Trump’s approval rating has fallen from 40 per cent to 33 per cent since the conflict began, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling, as rising gas prices have undercut his 2024 campaign promise to lower costs for Americans.
Trump, who campaigned on a promise to end wars, has argued that Iran’s missile buildup and nuclear ambitions required action, but he has not persuaded most voters. Just 31 per cent of the country approve of the conflict, according to the polling. That’s a lower number than other recent U.S. conflicts at a similar stage, including the war in Afghanistan, which had approval ratings above 50 per cent for years in Gallup polls.
Voter anger over high prices poses a problem for Trump’s Republican Party before November’s midterm elections, when it must defend narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress.
The conflict has also widened a rift between more isolationist Republicans, who want to see a quick end, and Republican lawmakers who believe Trump should keep military pressure on Tehran.
2. The war has shaken the global economy – but less than feared
The U.S. and Israeli attacks triggered immediate alarm because the Strait of Hormuz – which narrows to about 34 km wide between Iran and Oman – carries roughly a fifth of the world’s energy supplies. The disruption sent oil prices sharply higher and prompted fears of a global downturn.
The damage has been significant but less severe than many economists initially feared. The International Monetary Fund has cut its global growth forecast twice since the war began and now expects the world economy to grow by 3.0 per cent this year, compared with its 3.3 per cent forecast in January.
Still, the global economy has proved more resilient than during the oil shocks of the 1970s. Major economies are less energy-intensive than they were then, and strong spending and investment – including a continuing boom in artificial intelligence – have helped cushion the blow.
3. Iran is wounded but not defeated
Iran’s military and economy have suffered severe damage, but Tehran can still launch attacks and keep the Strait of Hormuz closed.
In May, the top U.S. military commander for the Middle East, Admiral Brad Cooper, told Congress that U.S. forces had destroyed 161 Iranian naval vessels and disabled 82 per cent of its air-defence systems. He said Iran’s air force, which had previously flown up to 100 sorties a day, was no longer conducting missions.
Even so, Iran retains drones and missiles and has successfully attacked shipping and U.S. military installations around the region.
In March, Reuters reported that the United States could determine with certainty that it has destroyed only about a third of Iran’s vast missile arsenal. The status of around another third was less clear but bombings likely damaged, destroyed or buried those missiles in underground tunnels and bunkers, sources told Reuters at the time.

Flash flooding along the Himalayan border between Nepal and China, caused by a glacial collapse, has killed at least 570 people. Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said the number of Canadians and permanent residents missing in the region is now 32.
No Canadians are among the 121 foreign nationals the Nepal Tourism Board said Friday had been rescued.
Canada’s $5 million contribution will go toward organizations like the Red Cross to deliver life-saving assistance to people on the ground.
Global Affairs Canada has deployed five consular officials to Kathmandu to support Canadians and work with local officials, and Anand said more can be deployed if needed.

But that optimistic view from Dominic LeBlanc, who raised the prospect of a “mutually beneficial” trade deal on Thursday, less than a week after negotiations fell apart, was quickly derailed by U.S. President Donald Trump’s declaration that he was renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America.
The minister was responding to comments made a day earlier by his main negotiating partner, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, who said that while the American side raised concerns about Canadian policies that urge online streaming companies to promote French programming, it did not insist on changes.

“Canada welcomes that the U.S. is now withdrawing its positions on discoverability and labelling and is confirming that measures to promote French language and Canadian culture will not be subject to future U.S. trade actions,” Mr. LeBlanc said Thursday in a post on X.
“We look forward to further constructive U.S. clarifications on their other positions, which would create the possibility of a mutually beneficial trade agreement that respects Canadian sovereignty.”
Mr. Greer had made the comments in a Wednesday interview with CBC News, during which he acknowledged Canadian frustrations.
“Our view is, you know, don’t retaliate. But I know how people are feeling in Canada and what they think,” he said.
Mr. Trump did not maintain that tone during a Thursday afternoon White House news conference, where he signed an executive order next to a map showing Lake Ontario renamed as Lake America.
“This is official, effective immediately,” he said.
Last year, Mr. Trump declared that the U.S. was renaming the Gulf of Mexico, saying it was in the country’s national interest.
“We changed it, and now it’s very routinely called the Gulf of America. So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean. So maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific,” he said.
During the news conference, Mr. Trump repeated some of his past grievances with Ottawa, including claims that Canada’s auto policies are unfair and that the country does not spend enough on its military.
“Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade,” he said.
On Mr. Trump’s lake renaming, Prime Minister Mark Carney responded with a post on X.
“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.’
“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America. We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded with a social-media post: “It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever.”
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew dismissed the President’s announcement.

Harley-Davidson becomes unlikely flashpoint in Canada-U.S. trade war
Miller does not expect the tariff’s effects to influence major business decisions until early next year
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Few brands symbolize American freedom and rebellion quite like Harley-Davidson.
The 123-year-old company is headquartered in Milwaukee and operates its largest U.S. manufacturing plant in York, Pennsylvania. Amid U.S. President Donald Trump’s global tariff campaign — aimed at reshoring production to American shores — Harley-Davidson announced in June that it would return production of some products from Thailand to U.S. facilities.
That announcement came before the U.S. administration announced the Section 301 and Section 338 tariffs, and before Ottawa unveiled its retaliation against those measures and earlier Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminum. If Canada implements duties on September 8, as planned, it would introduce a 50 per cent tariff on U.S.-origin motorcycle imports to Canada larger than 800cc with internal-combustion engines.
Ottawa said its list of tariffs was crafted to protect the “domestic market share for Canadian companies,” rather than to target politically sensitive products in U.S. battleground states ahead of November’s midterms, but affecting Harley motorcycles could have political implications in at least one swing district: Pennsylvania’s 10th, a highly competitive congressional seat.
While the Canadian tariff does not name Harley-Davidson, it is expected to cover many Harley models made in the United States. So while the company is being held up as evidence that Trump’s tariff strategy can bring manufacturing back to the United States, Canada’s 50 per cent tariff on motorcycles could test whether reshored factories can thrive when a major trading partner makes its products more expensive.
Canada accounted for roughly 5 per cent of Harley-Davidson’s global retail motorcycle sales last year, with 6,434 motorcycles sold north of the border. That means the tariff’s direct effect on the company may be limited — but its political symbolism could be larger.
“If production is reshored to the United States, then what form does it get reshored?” asked Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a trade policy analyst at the Cato Institute. “How many jobs are you actually creating? What kinds of jobs are you creating?”
“If there is to an extent a certain reliance on Canadian parts … the fact that this product is tariffed and the fact that some inputs could be tariffed … could affect the prospect of reshoring it more extensively and creating jobs,” he said.
Harley said the move would return machining, powertrain assembly, painting and final assembly for its Revolution Max platform to U.S. facilities serving the North American market. Production is expected to begin as early as next year, and the company says the move will support “dozens of additional American manufacturing and union jobs.” It has not said how many net new jobs will be created.
“If you have production in a country where there’s very little U.S. value added, and then that production moves to the U.S., that will overall be a net gain for manufacturing in the U.S. for that specific product category,” said Jason Miller, a supply chain management professor at Michigan State University.
“But it may not be a net gain for overall jobs in the U.S. if that means less demand for that broader product, and therefore less employment in the distribution side,” he added.
“A lot of the manufacturing jobs that were lost were not necessarily because of offshoring to other countries, but because of technological changes,” Obregon said, noting that the advent of advanced robotics could mean that reshoring production means fewer jobs.

items.body_text:
'All of a sudden the rug was pulled out': How Coyote vs. Acme went from the shelf to the big screen
In 2022, the cast and crew of Coyote vs. Acme attended a “funeral screening.”
It was as grim as it sounds. Warner Bros. had already announced the finished film was going to be forever shelved. Studio execs had controversially decided to take a $30-million tax writeoff as a cost-saving exercise rather than take on the expense of releasing and distributing it.
The film’s stars, Will Forte and Lana Condor, were among those went to the screening. The mood was not jubilant, to say the least, even though everyone was impressed with what they saw on the screen.
“That experience of watching the film was very layered,” says Condor, in a Zoom interview with Postmedia alongside Forte. “We came in very confused and angry and thinking ‘well maybe, the film isn’t as great as we thought it was going to be … ‘”
“The shoot went great, we had been hearing the post-process was great, they were already testing it and the testing was going great,” adds Forte. “All of a sudden the rug was pulled out.”
“And so then when we watched the film and the credits rolled, there was this mass confusion and anger,” Condor says. “When credits rolled, we were like ‘This is a great movie! How is this possible?’”
After facing significant backlash and negative media coverage, the studio execs changed their minds and allowed an outside distributor to purchase the film. Enter Ketchup Entertainment, an independent film company that picked it up and held another screening before its wide release on Aug. 28.
The feeling was different the second time around.
“That was a great watch because we knew it was going to come out and it’s a great movie,” Condor says.
This strange chapter in the film’s behind-the-scenes story is being seen by some commentators as an indictment of the tone-deaf corporate indifference that seems to have overrun Hollywood studios these days. It is also strangely fitting for the tone of Coyote Vs. Acme, a story about corporate indifference and underdogs who never give up. Further vindication has come from early reviews, which have been largely positive. “Consistently funny and clever” proclaimed Brian Tallerico of rogerebert.com. “A cracking comedy that’s easily among the top ‘Looney Tunes’ movies ever,” writes Johnny Oleksinksi in the New York Post. “It’s smart, silly, and ultimately inspiring,” says Kristy Puchko of Mashable.com.
Directed by Dave Green and based on a satirical 1990 New Yorker article by Ian Frazier, Coyote vs. Acme blends animation and live-action in the spirit of Who Framed Roger Rabbit? Its central plot revolves around Wile E. Coyote’s decision to sue Acme, the massive corporation behind the endless trail of shoddy equipment he has used in his tireless pursuit of the Road Runner. He enlists the sad-eyed and defeated Kevin Avery (Forte) to represent him, an ambulance-chasing lawyer who specializes in getting small, out-of-court settlements from Acme for cartoon characters.
Avery is joined by his idealistic niece, Paige (played by Condor), who possesses unyielding enthusiasm and optimism for the case even though it pits them against a behemoth and heartless corporation fronted by a ruthless lawyer (played by former pro-wrestler Jon Cena).
“That experience of watching the film was very layered. We came in very confused and angry and thinking ‘well maybe, the film isn’t as great as we thought it was going to be … ‘
The mute Coyote shifts from the antagonist of the Looney Tunes shorts to a somewhat sympathetic character whose steadfast belief in his own genius despite years of failure becomes the endearing centre of the film. What follows is a story about friendship, loyalty and perseverance filled with slapstick humour, heart and appearances by a long line of Looney Tunes favourites. That includes everything from significant roles for Foghorn Leghorn and Tweety Bird to savvy bits featuring cameos by Pepe Le Pew, Gossamer and Dr. Lorre.

items.title: ‘Lake Ontario’ hat maker sees politics and sales in Trump’s name change
items.summary: Ottawa-based Jackpine took about 100 orders for 'Lake Ontario' caps shortly after launching the product online in response to Trump’s threats
items.body_text:
'Lake Ontario' hat maker sees politics and sales in Trump's name change
Ottawa-based Jackpine took about 100 orders for 'Lake Ontario' caps shortly after launching the product online in response to Trump’s threats
Mere hours before President Donald Trump signed an order to change Lake Ontario’s name on US maps, a husband-and-wife team in Canada’s capital city began marketing a blue hat with its name.
If retail is detail, the timing for Liam Mooney and Emma Cochrane was nearly perfect. Their firm, Ottawa-based Jackpine, took about 100 orders for “Lake Ontario” caps shortly after launching the product online in response to Trump’s threats to rename the body of water “Lake America.”
Jackpine is preparing to sell thousands more — expecting a sharp public reaction now that Trump has signed a directive to rename the Great Lake that separates Ontario and New York.
“Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade,” Trump told reporters when asked what message he was sending to the US’s northern neighbor. “They want to be treated like they’re a state, and so we just can’t do that anymore.”
Trump’s idea to rename the lake was part of a public feud with Ontario Premier Doug Ford. Each leader insulted the other in media appearances and on social media this week after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed.
Mooney called the lake renaming “absurd,” but also saw the more serious implications. “It’s this sort of annexation rhetoric made real,” he said. “There’s a realpolitik to this thing.”
Jackpine will ship the first Lake Ontario hats within two weeks to buyers in both countries, including people in upstate New York, Illinois and border communities.
Their online apparel store became a sensation in Canada after Trump won the 2024 election and began musing about turning the northern country into the 51st state. Jackpine designed “Canada is not for sale” hats, which imitate the look of Make America Great Again headgear, except on a blue background.
Demand spiked after Ford wore a “Canada is not for sale” hat to a Canadian political conference. The company sold 50,000 of them, according to Mooney.
The name Lake Ontario is more than 400 years old, “predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a post on X. “We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
“It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever,” Doug Ford said.
The Lake Ontario caps, which include a biodegradable brim that Mooney said is safe for aquatic life, are being made in Sherbrooke, Quebec, and finished in Ottawa.
Polling shows Canadians are largely united behind Carney’s tough approach to negotiations with the US. Mooney said early orders suggest a cross-country reaction to renaming the lake, as he’s already sold Lake Ontario hats to customers in rural Alberta and Manitoba — thousands of miles away.

items.body_text:
Rattrapé par la Coalition avenir Québec (CAQ) dans un premier sondage en trois ans, le Parti québécois (PQ) s’est rendu jeudi où devait naître l’usine de Northvolt pour tenter de rappeler aux électeurs « la dilapidation des fonds publics » par les gouvernements Legault-Fréchette. « Les Québécois en ont soupé et ils veulent du changement », estime Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.
Tout près de la clôture encadrant l’immense terrain vague qui enjambe McMasterville et Saint-Basile-le-Grand, le chef péquiste a réitéré sa promesse de mettre fin aux « subventions tous azimuts » aux multinationales étrangères et d’utiliser cet argent pour financer une baisse de deux points de pourcentage sur l’impôt des sociétés.
S’il est porté au pouvoir le 5 octobre, il s’engage à rabaisser le fardeau fiscal des petites et moyennes entreprises de 11,5 % à 9,5 % sur une période de quatre ans. Concrètement, calcule-t-il, une compagnie ayant déclaré un revenu imposable de 5 millions de dollars effectuerait donc des économies de 90 000 $.
Devant les journalistes, le chef péquiste a rappelé qu’il souhaitait abolir le Fonds de développement économique, une caisse financée par le ministère de l’Économie et qui permet au gouvernement de distribuer des subventions. En coupant court à ce qu’il appelle « le bar ouvert des subventions aux multinationales étrangères », il pense pouvoir financer sa promesse « à coût nul ».
« Ça correspondant à un retrait de 2 milliards dans les subventions tous azimuts », a-t-il plaidé. Le coût brut de la baisse d’impôts proposée serait quant à lui situé entre 2 milliards et 2,4 milliards sur quatre ans, a par la suite précisé son équipe.
L’annonce du PQ survient deux jours après que le chef conservateur, Éric Duhaime, a lui aussi annoncé une baisse d’impôts de 59 % pour les PME.
Le PQ et la CAQ presque à égalité
« PSPP » avait choisi de commencer sa journée devant ce qui devait être Northvolt car l’investissement de Québec dans l’usine de batteries est, d’après lui, le « symbole » ultime du « gaspillage » des deniers publics par les gouvernements caquistes des deux derniers mandats.
« Pendant 8 ans, la CAQ, avec [les ministres consécutifs de l’Économie] Pierre Fitzgibbon et Christine Fréchette, ont fait à leur tête et ont distribué les chèques au pif », a-t-il déploré, quelques heures après qu’un sondage Synopsis-La Presse eut placé son parti à quasi-égalité avec celui de Mme Fréchette.
Le chef péquiste ne s’en fait pas trop avec le coup de sonde, qui accorde 28 % des intentions de vote au PQ contre 27 % pour la CAQ. « Je pense qu’avant de commenter ce sondage-là, je vais attendre d’autres sondages », a-t-il dit. « Ce qu’on a vu plus souvent, ce sont [les maisons de sondage] Léger et Pallas, au cours des dernières années. »
Contacté par Le Devoir, l’analyste de sondages et fondateur du site Qc125, Philippe J. Fournier, a qualifié Synopsis de « fiable ». « Ça fait plusieurs années qu’ils sondent le Québec », a-t-il écrit.

items.title: Une tranchée de 1711 refait surface à Québec
items.summary: Le fossé aurait été creusé il y a plus de 300 ans pour résister à l’expédition Walker.
items.body_text:
Les archéologues de la Ville de Québec auraient découvert les traces d’un fossé creusé en 1711 pour résister à l’invasion de l’amiral britannique Hovenden Walker. Le vestige d’une trentaine de mètres de long a été mis au jour à l’emplacement du futur pôle d’échanges du tramway dans le quartier Saint-Roch.
« Considérant l’envergure de l’ouvrage, il serait surprenant qu’il soit associé à un simple fossé de drainage ou à toute autre structure », lit-on dans le rapport de fouilles obtenu par Le Devoir. L’hypothèse des archéologues a été validée par la superposition de son tracé sur les cartes du XVIIIe siècle.
La tranchée a été découverte en 2025 à l’ombre de l’ancienne passerelle de l’autoroute Laurentienne. Elle correspondrait au fossé de l’un des deux demi-bastions et de la courtine aménagés en 1711 dans la partie la plus étroite de la pointe aux Lièvres, qui formait autrefois une presqu’île.
Ce retranchement se prolongeait sur près d’un kilomètre en suivant la rive sud de la rivière Saint-Charles jusqu’aux abords de la gare du Palais actuelle. Une seconde ligne de défense avait été mise en place au nord de ce cours d’eau, dans la plaine de la Canardière aujourd’hui occupée par les quartiers du Vieux-Limoilou, de Maizeret et de Giffard.
Le naufrage d’une partie des navires de l’amiral Walker sur les rochers de la Côte-Nord dans la nuit du 3 septembre 1711 n’aura pas permis de tester l’efficacité de ces ouvrages creusés dans l’urgence par les soldats français et les miliciens canadiens. Sans cette tragédie maritime ayant fait près d’un millier de victimes, c’est sur le bord de la Saint-Charles que se serait joué le sort de la Nouvelle-France, 50 ans avant sa conquête effective.
Autodidacte
Les retranchements de 1711 ont été dessinés par l’officier d’infanterie Josué de Beaucours, un vétéran du siège de Québec de 1690. « Il n’était pas ingénieur en tant que tel, mais il avait une très grande connaissance des fortifications », explique l’historien André Charbonneau. Le retraité de Parcs Canada le soupçonne d’avoir acquis les bases du métier auprès du célèbre Vauban, qu’il a côtoyé brièvement à Brest dans les années 1680.
Beaucours est moins connu que Chaussegros de Léry, à qui l’on doit les remparts actuels de Québec. L’ingénieur autodidacte a néanmoins fait la une des journaux en 2018 lors de la découverte de ce que l’on croyait être un segment de son rempart palissadé érigé en 1693 à l’ouest de la haute ville de Québec. La structure, qui est aujourd’hui exposée au Musée de la civilisation, serait plutôt une canalisation du XVIIIe siècle.
Parmi les legs durables de Beaucours toujours visibles de la capitale, on note la redoute du cap Diamant, qui a été intégrée à la citadelle, le cavalier du Moulin et la redoute Dauphine. Cette dernière a toutefois dû être consolidée par d’imposants contreforts sous le régime britannique afin d’éviter que la structure ne glisse au bas de la côte où elle avait été construite !
« Beaucours n’avait pas la même expérience que les autres ingénieurs », souligne André Charbonneau en prenant soin de ne pas trop critiquer le bâtisseur décédé en 1750 à l’âge avancé de 88 ans. « Ses ouvrages n’étaient pas toujours adaptés à la topographie. »
Brèche
Beaucours a laissé des plans de son retranchement de la rivière Saint-Charles. L’un d’eux présente la coupe longitudinale de cette fortification dotée d’un fossé triangulaire servant à briser l’assaut de l’ennemi évoluant sous les tirs des défenseurs postés à l’abri d’un parapet formé d’un talus.
Pour franchir ce type d’ouvrage, les assaillants devaient sauter dans le fossé afin d’attaquer le parapet à coups de pelles et de pioches. « Lorsque la brèche sera faite, les travailleurs abandonneront leurs outils et, reprenant leurs armes, ils monteront tous ensemble la baïonnette au but du fusil en criant “tue, tue” », indique le capitaine Jean Louis Le Cointe dans un manuel d’instruction paru au milieu du XVIIIe siècle.

items.title: Un Rwandais condamné à perpétuité aux Pays-Bas pour sa participation au génocide
items.summary: Les enquêteurs néerlandais se penchent sur son cas depuis 2020 et ont interrogé des dizaines de témoins.
items.body_text:
Un tribunal néerlandais a condamné vendredi à la perpétuité un Rwandais pour avoir participé au massacre de 3000 Tutsis lors du génocide de 1994.
« Les infractions commises par l’accusé ont profondément choqué la société. Il s’agit d’une atteinte considérable à l’ordre juridique au Rwanda et dans le monde entier », a déclaré un juge du tribunal du district de La Haye.
« Seule une peine d’emprisonnement à perpétuité est justifiée. C’est donc la peine que nous allons prononcer », a-t-il poursuivi.
Outre sa participation au massacre, Eugène N., 66 ans, a été reconnu coupable de s’être livré à une « vague de pillages et de destructions », incendiant des maisons et saccageant des biens.
Au cours de violences qui ont eu lieu en avril 1994, environ 3000 victimes ayant cherché refuge dans un stade de foot à Mbazi, dans le sud du Rwanda, avaient été massacrées.
« Le suspect a lui-même lancé une grenade dans un stade où se trouvaient des hommes, des femmes et des enfants » avait lancé la procureure lors d’une audience devant le tribunal en juin.
« Si les crimes effroyables commis par le suspect, au cours desquels non pas une seule, mais environ 3000 personnes innocentes ont été littéralement massacrées […] ne méritent pas la prison à perpétuité, alors quels faits le méritent ? », avait-elle ajouté.
Eugène N. a toutefois été acquitté du chef d’accusation d’incitation au génocide le concernant, les juges n’ayant trouvé aucune preuve concluante.
Mandat d’arrêt international
Eugène N. a nié ces accusations et a déclaré aux juges qu’il avait lui-même été victime de violences.
« Je n’ai commis aucun des faits qui me sont reprochés », avait-il affirmé, la voix déformée et le visage caché à la demande de la défense, pour des raisons de sécurité. « Je n’aurais pas pu prendre part à ces événements au cours desquels des membres de ma famille ont également été tués. »
Plus de 800 000 personnes selon l’ONU, essentiellement des membres de la minorité tutsi, ont été tuées au printemps 1994.
D’après les autorités néerlandaises, le suspect était recherché depuis longtemps par le parquet rwandais, qui avait émis un mandat d’arrêt international à son encontre en 2014. Ayant acquis la nationalité néerlandaise et résidant aux Pays-Bas depuis 1998, il ne peut néanmoins être extradé vers le Rwanda.
Les enquêteurs néerlandais se penchent sur son cas depuis 2020 et ont interrogé des dizaines de témoins, y compris au Rwanda.
Des tribunaux de pays européens ont jugé et condamné plusieurs dizaines de personnes impliquées dans le génocide au Rwanda en vertu du principe de compétence universelle, qui leur permet de juger les crimes les plus graves, même s’ils ont été commis à l’étranger.

items.title: García Luna corruption case wins $5.8M for Guerrero schools: Friday’s mañanera recapped
items.summary: At Friday's mañanera, Sheinbaum said funds diverted by García Luna will return to Mexico to aid Guerrero schools, declared the country is doing "very well," and congratulated a gold medal-winning rower. The post García Luna corruption case wins $5.8M for Guerrero schools: Friday’s mañanera recapped appeared first on Mexico News Daily
items.body_text:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds
- 💰 García Luna case yields $5.8M for Guerrero schools: UIF chief Omar Reyes Colmenares said Mexico received US $5.8 million this week from its civil suit victory over the Weinberg family — ex-Security Minister García Luna’s alleged frontmen — in a Miami-Dade court. Sheinbaum said the funds will go to schools in Guerrero’s disadvantaged Montaña region.
- 🇲🇽 Mexico is ‘Doing very well,’ Sheinbaum says ahead of second report: Sheinbaum declared Mexico is “doing very well” almost two years into her six-year term. Her positive assessment of the current state of affairs came ahead of the presentation of her second annual government report next Tuesday.
- 🚣 Gold for rower Kenia Lechuga: Sheinbaum congratulated Nuevo León native Kenia Lechuga on her gold medal in the women’s lightweight sculls at the 2026 World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam, saying that as a former rower herself she felt “special affection” for the win. Mexican rowers also won gold in the women’s lightweight double sculls and bronze in the men’s lightweight sculls.
Why today’s mañanera matters
Today’s mañanera was significant as the federal government was able to demonstrate that its successful civil suit against former Security Minister Genaro García Luna — now imprisoned in the United States — is reaping monetary rewards.
Also of note was President Claudia Sheinbaum’s positive assessment of the current state of affairs in Mexico almost two years into her six-year term. Her favorable evaluation of the prevailing situation came four days before she is scheduled to present her second annual government report (segundo informe de gobierno) in a speech in Mexico City.
Sheinbaum: US $5.8 million recovered in García Luna case to go to schools in Guerrero
Omar Reyes Colmenares, head of the federal government’s Financial Intelligence Unit (UIF), told reporters that on Tuesday of this week, Mexico received US $5.8 million in funds recovered in the case involving García Luna, who in 2024 was sentenced to 38 years in prison in the United States after he was found guilty of collusion with the Sinaloa Cartel.
He noted that the UIF filed a civil suit in Florida aimed at recovering public money that was diverted out of Mexico in a corruption scheme involving García Luna and members of the Weinberg family. Members of the Weinberg family have been identified as frontmen for García Luna, who served as security minister during the 2006-12 government led by former President Felipe Calderón.
Reyes highlighted that a court in Miami handed down a ruling in May in favor of the Mexican state and against the Weinberg family. As part of the ruling, Judge Lisa Walsh in Miami-Dade County ordered members of the Weinberg family and related companies to pay US $578.5 million in damages to the Mexican state for losses incurred as a result of their involvement in corruption schemes.
“As a result of this process,” said Reyes, “the Mexican state received US $5.8 million on Aug. 25, 2026.”
Miami court awards Mexico an additional US $578.5M in damages from García Luna’s corruption schemes
The UIF chief said the money was obtained from the recovery of a surety bond and “the liquidation of 12 properties located in Florida, United States, and linked to the Weinberg family.” He noted that Mexico is awaiting the liquidation of other assets in order to recover additional funds diverted out of the country by García Luna.
Later in the press conference, Sheinbaum said that the $5.8 million in recovered funds that Mexico received this week would be allocated to schools in the Montaña region of the southern state of Guerrero.
“It’s around 100 million pesos that is going to be used in [one of] the most disadvantaged areas in the country,” she said.
