items.title: Dutch court jails man for life over role in Rwanda genocide
items.summary: "Only a lifelong prison sentence does justice to the immense suffering that has been inflicted on the victims and the bereaved families," said the court.
items.body_text:
Audio By Vocalize
A Dutch court on Friday handed a life sentence to a 66-year-old man for his role in the massacre of 3,000 Tutsis during the 1994 Rwanda genocide.
During the violence that took place in April 1994, terrified victims sought refuge in a football stadium in Mbazi, southern Rwanda, only to be systematically slaughtered.
The judge said that the man, identified as Eugene N., prevented Tutsis from escaping the stadium and threw a grenade into the crowd.
The court said he was also involved in attacks preceding the stadium massacre, when houses were looted and set on fire.
"Only a lifelong prison sentence does justice to the immense suffering that has been inflicted on the victims and the bereaved families," said the court.
His actions were committed with "genocidal intent," said the presiding judge handing down the verdict.
He was convicted of war crimes and the crime of genocide.
At hearings in June before the District Court of The Hague, prosecutors had urged a life sentence, saying that N. was "personally involved" in the killings.
"If the horrific crimes of the suspect -- in which not one but an estimated 3,000 innocent people were literally slaughtered, in which the suspect personally threw a grenade into a stadium... do not deserve a life sentence, then what does?" one prosecutor asked the court.
The 1994 Rwandan genocide claimed the lives of an estimated 800,000 people over the course of three months. According to UN figures, most of the victims were part of the Tutsi minority in Rwanda.
The suspect had denied the charges, saying he himself was a victim who had lost dozens of his own relatives in what he described as "those horrific events".
N.'s lawyers had urged an acquittal on all counts, saying their client in fact did "everything to prevent the genocide".
"The case has torn his scars open again. He is a broken man," said one of the defence lawyers during the trial.
According to local news agency ANP, the defence said they will "almost certainly appeal the charges".
'Multiple severe crimes'
Stay informed. Subscribe to our newsletter
At the time of the massacres, N. held a position of responsibility in the community, said the court, overseeing around 1,000 people in Mbazi.
"The suspect was a man who was held in high regard and he must have been aware of his role and the influence he had as a local authority," said the court.
"Instead of staying on the sidelines, the defendant committed multiple severe crimes," added the court.
The court said he watched from a road as his men stormed into houses of Tutsis, setting them ablaze.
He was however acquitted of the charge of incitement to genocide.
- fled to the Netherlands in 1998. Rwandan authorities issued an international arrest warrant for him in 2014.
However, according to Dutch law, he cannot be extradited as he has obtained nationality in the Netherlands.
Dutch prosecutors opened their own investigation in 2020 and have since interviewed dozens of witnesses in Rwanda. N. was arrested in 2024.
European courts have tried and convicted several dozen people involved in the Rwanda genocide under the principle of universal jurisdiction, which allows them to hear the most serious crimes even if committed abroad.

items.title: Iran says still open to diplomacy as war with US hits six months
items.summary: "Putting diplomacy back on track isn't impossible. It hinges on US understanding of one simple fact: pressure doesn't work," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said.
items.body_text:
Audio By Vocalize
Iran left the door open to diplomacy on Friday, six months into a war with the United States that has upended the Middle East, but only if Washington abandons its pressure campaign.
"Putting diplomacy back on track isn't impossible. It hinges on US understanding of one simple fact: pressure doesn't work," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X on Friday.
Diplomatic efforts, spearheaded by mediators including Pakistan and Qatar, have tried for months to bring an end to the war started by the US and Israel in late February to no avail.
While a ceasefire was agreed in April and a memorandum of understanding towards a final peace deal was signed in June, no agreement has been forthcoming and Washington has since declared "economic warfare" against Tehran.
In the latest effort to reinvigorate diplomacy, Araghchi met his Qatari counterpart on Thursday in the Iranian capital to discuss the Strait of Hormuz, closed by the Islamic republic at the start of the war, at the tail end of a week of intense Iranian talks with Oman and Pakistan.
A US naval counter-blockade of Iranian ports is squeezing petrol supplies in Iran, amid a shortfall of domestic production, as the US ramps up pressure on its foe, declaring an "economic D-Day".
The April ceasefire put an end to the most intense fighting, but sporadic attacks, mainly around the Strait of Hormuz, have dimmed the prospects of a final peace agreement.
'Build trust'
Tehran has for weeks been holding talks on the future of Hormuz with Muscat, whose territorial waters account for the other half of the strait, while insisting that Hormuz will remain closed so long as Washington has not fulfilled its commitments under the June memorandum, which calls for lifting the US counter-blockade and removing sanctions.
"The US should build trust, speak respectfully, acknowledge our rights, and uphold commitments," Araghchi said.
Iranian lawmaker Esmail Kowsari reiterated to state television on Friday that if the memorandum was not implemented and the US "does not respect its commitments, not only will the Strait of Hormuz remain closed, but the United States must be ready for our offensive actions and we will seek them in the most distant places".
While Washington now aims to crush Iran economically, Tehran has weathered decades of international sanctions and experts remain sceptical about how much more pressure the US can bring to bear.
Analysts say the US plan to isolate Iran would require unlikely cooperation from trading partner China, which has defended its cooperation with Tehran and vowed to safeguard its interests.
China remains able to buy Iranian crude, an important source of revenue for Tehran, via overland routes not reliant on the Strait of Hormuz.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said "no one is above the reach of US sanctions" when asked if Washington would target Chinese banks that do business with Iran, ahead of an expected September visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping to the US capital.

items.title: Ghana: Ghana's Kente Protection Opens New Economic Possibilities
items.summary: [Bird Story Agency] Ghana's geographical indication for kente could help weavers protect the celebrated cloth from imitation, reach new markets and earn more from generations of skill. Turning legal recognition into livelihoods will require collective standards, business support and the revival of local raw-material production.
items.body_text:
Ghana’s geographical indication for kente could help weavers protect the celebrated cloth from imitation, reach new markets and earn more from generations of skill. Turning legal recognition into livelihoods will require collective standards, business support and the revival of local raw-material production.
It is early morning in Ziope, in Ghana’s Agotime-Kpetoe District, 22 kilometres east of the Volta regional capital, Ho. After sweeping his work area, Emmanuel Kofi Atsisey says a prayer, arranges his threads by colour and organises his tools. He then settles onto a self-made folding stool attached to his loom and begins using both hands and feet to create a design.
Income from the craft he began learning 21 years ago helps Atsisey support his family and pay the bills. He is now considering taking his skills to neighbouring Burkina Faso in the hope of earning more.
“The same kente we sell here in Ghana for about GH¢2,500 (US225) can go for more than GH¢4,000 (US360) when converted from CFA francs. I even thought of relocating there if the opportunity is real,” he says, recalling a conversation with a contact there.
Kente weaving is often passed down within families, but Atsisey took a different route. He entered a formal apprenticeship with a master weaver before becoming an independent artisan.
Kente embodies generations of knowledge passed down through skilled artisans. Its patterns tell stories of power, dignity, wealth and community identity, and the cloth is often worn on significant occasions.
Coming from one of Ghana’s major kente-producing areas, Atsisey has spent years combining tradition with innovation. Although he says earnings do not reflect the labour involved, the fabric’s global standing gives him pride.
“Even if you push yourself, you may produce only one or two pieces. More complex designs take four to six weeks to complete a set,” he explains.
Alongside established patterns, Atsisey creates original designs that reflect both cultural continuity and personal creativity.
“The block in Fatia kente is called Sukluikpe — sugar cubes. I designed it differently and named it ‘Life is sweet’. I have created many designs myself,” he says. Known fully as "Fatia Fata Nkrumah" kente cloth, it translates from the Akan language to "Fatia befits Nkrumah." Fatia was the wife of Ghana's first President, Dr. Kwame Nkrumah from Egypt.
Kente’s growing presence in contemporary fashion at national and international events is encouraging artisans and entrepreneurs to see the cloth as both cultural heritage and an economic asset.
According to the Annual Non-Traditional Export Statistics Report by the Ghana Export Promotion Authority (GEPA), the country’s industrial arts and crafts subsector recorded 23% export growth in 2024. GEPA said the export value of Kente products rose to US $38,901.83 in 2024, compared to US $6,256.00 in 2023, representing growth of 522% and an indication of rising international demand for Ghanaian textiles.
As demand grows, artisans in production centres are also working to protect the historic fabric’s authenticity.
At 27, traditional textile artisan Richmond Quarshie, from Agbozume in southeastern Ghana’s Volta Region, is part of his family’s weaving business. The income helped support him through secondary school.
“I started around 19,” he says. “All my brothers are involved. It is the work we inherited.”
Quarshie learnt the craft from his two older brothers and specialised in the Bonwire style of kente for customers in the Ashanti Region. After completing school, weaving became his main livelihood.
“For now, I’m working for someone,” he says. “I don’t have the capital to start on my own. That’s my biggest challenge.”
Quarshie believes the government could help by creating structured employment and production systems. He also points to the cost of imported thread as a barrier, underscoring the need for local production support as Ghana seeks to strengthen its manufacturing sector.

items.title: Benin: How Benin Is Turning Its Cotton Wealth Into An Industrial Economy
items.summary: [Bird Story Agency] Benin is using its position as West Africa's largest cotton producer to pursue a bigger economic prize: processing more of what it grows at home. At the Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone (GDIZ), cotton is being turned into fabrics and garments, creating jobs and retaining value that previously left the country with the trade of raw fibres. Its progress offers an emerging model for industrialisation for the continent.
items.body_text:
Benin is using its position as West Africa’s largest cotton producer to pursue a bigger economic prize: processing more of what it grows at home. At the Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone (GDIZ), cotton is being turned into fabrics and garments, creating jobs and retaining value that previously left the country with the trade of raw fibres. Its progress offers an emerging model for industrialisation for the continent.
At the Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone, about 45 kilometres north of Cotonou, young workers such as team leader Inès Alowakinnou are gaining experience in an industry that barely existed at this scale a few years ago. Their work lies at the centre of Benin’s ambitious attempt to turn its cotton wealth into factories, formal employment and a more diversified economy.
“Working conditions are good, I’m gaining experience, and I wouldn’t hesitate to encourage any young person to follow my example,” says Alowakinnou, who works in the industrial engineering department.
According to the IMF 2024 Country Report, Benin's exports have been mainly concentrated in commodities such as cotton and cashews, accounting for more than one third of total export between 2016 and 2021 (before adjusting for informal trade flows).
Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines
For Benin Textile Corporation maintenance supervisor, Manfaz Lamidi, the satisfaction comes from maintaining production and solving technical breakdowns and defects. Their experiences reflect the larger ambition behind GDIZ: to transform Benin from an exporter of raw agricultural commodities into a manufacturer and seller of higher-value products.
Benin harvested 533,590 tonnes of seed cotton during the 2025/26 season, regaining its position as the leading producer in the CFA franc zone. But producing large volumes of cotton does not automatically deliver the full economic value of the crop. That value increases as fibre moves through ginning, spinning, weaving, knitting, dyeing, garment production, branding and retail.
GDIZ is attempting to bring more of those stages inside Benin.
“For many decades, most African countries have always exported raw commodities without any value addition. But in Benin, we have decided to take matters into our own hands to change that paradigm so that we can create more wealth and jobs out of our natural resources,” says GDIZ CEO Létondji Beheton.
The foundations of the GDIZ model's success
GDIZ is a public-private partnership between Benin and industrial infrastructure developer Arise Integrated Industrial Platforms (ARISE IIP) covers a planned 1,640 hectares, with 400 hectares allocated to its first phase. Construction started in 2021.
Although cotton and textiles are central to its operations, the zone is also intended to process locally produced cashew nuts, soybeans, maize and other agricultural commodities, and mineral resources such as clay, kaolin, granite, etc.
“We do not copy and paste in Benin,” Beheton says. “What we do, we look at other models and we create our own model, and this is what we have done here.”
For decades — since the first free zones emerged in the 1960s and 70s — the success of a Special Economic Zone was measured by its tax incentives. Today, industrial investors weigh reliable power, ready-built factory space, port access, and workforce training as much as tax breaks. The GDIZ has built its pitch around exactly these — a 1,640-hectare site with turnkey infrastructure, on-site logistics to the Port of Cotonou, and worker-training programs like Azôli, which has already placed more than 5,000 young people into factory jobs.
“In this zone, we have a single window counter where you have more than 17 public entities,” Beheton says, citing immigration, tax, customs and other government services. These are intended to give investors one point of contact in terms of all the paperwork that is needed for them to develop their business .

items.title: Africa: Africa Brought Deals to Washington - The Test is Whether the Money Moves
items.summary: [African Business] Washington, DC -- The inaugural Africa Business Investment Summit saw a target of $500m of structured commitments, a royal keynote and an unusually candid accounting of why capital still hesitates.
items.body_text:
Washington, DC — The inaugural Africa Business Investment Summit saw a target of $500m of structured commitments, a royal keynote and an unusually candid accounting of why capital still hesitates.
Otumfuo Osei Tutu II had been speaking for barely five minutes when he put the question the rest of the day would attempt to answer. The Asantehene looked out at the ballroom and asked why, given everything that had just been claimed for the continent, Africa is still not developed.
It was a striking thing to ask at a summit built to answer it. The Africa Business Investment Summit, convened for the first time by the Millennium Excellence Foundation under his patronage, gathered more than 500 delegates at MGM National Harbor in Oxon Hill, Maryland, on 27 and 28 August. It was designed, in the words of Ghana's Deputy Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, Sampson Ahi, as a deal-making arena, one in which discussion must lead to capital, capital to enterprise, and enterprise to jobs.
The organisers arrived with roughly $4 billion of opportunities and set themselves a smaller test: at least $500m in structured commitments, signed as memoranda of understanding and letters of intent before the delegates go home.
Speaking for President John Dramani Mahama, Ahi set the scene for the day's discussions with an update on Ghana's progress. He reported inflation down from 23.8% in December 2024 to 5.4% a year later, and 4.6% by July 2026. GDP grew 6% in 2025, the fastest since 2019, with non-oil growth at 7.6%, the highest in fourteen years. Foreign direct investment reached $2.62bn.
That last number is the registration figure. The balance of payments tells a subtler story. Net foreign direct investment on that measure was $1.91bn, and 95.4% of it came from reinvested earnings, leaving something in the order of $88m of genuinely new money arriving from abroad. Investors already in Ghana are staying and expanding. Persuading new ones through the door is the harder problem.
It is also the problem almost every session that followed was arguing about.
Reta Jo Lewis, the former president and chair of the Export-Import Bank of the United States, gave the most practical account. During her three years leading the agency, she said, its Africa portfolio went from $109m in 2022 to a record $3.6bn in authorisations across 2023 and 2024. The constraint was rarely capital. It was readiness.
She has little patience for the language investors use. "The minute somebody tells me, do you have a bankable project, I already know they're about to tell me they're not going to do my deal."
The financing conversation has to be part of a project's design, not a question asked after it. "Let's get to yes, not get to no."
Critical minerals
One area that is expected to drive Africa's development forward in the decades to come is exploitation of the continent's enormous critical minerals reserves.
Africa's mineral endowment is not in dispute and neither, said Ben Kincaid, chief executive of ReElement Technologies Africa, is the political will. Governments have written policies restricting the export of unprocessed material. What is missing is the midstream. Without regional refining capacity, a rule against exporting concentrate is unenforceable, because there is nowhere else for the concentrate to go.
Ayo Sopitan, chief executive of Metalex Commodities, which is building copper and cobalt production in Zambia, put the scale in perspective. By his count roughly 750 million tonnes of copper have been produced in all of human history, and the world will need about as much again within twenty-five years. The US Geological Survey's own estimate of cumulative production is nearer 700 million tonnes.

items.title: NCDC warns Nigerians as Cholera cases surpass 65,000 in 2026
items.summary: Mr Idris said the country is still in the rainy season, when cholera transmission can increase because flooding may contaminate water sources and overwhelm sanitation systems. The post NCDC warns Nigerians as Cholera cases surpass 65,000 in 2026 appeared first on Premium Times Nigeria.
items.body_text:
Nigeria has recorded more than 65,000 suspected cases of cholera across 35 states and approximately 195 local government areas this year, according to the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC).
The NCDC Director-General, Jide Idris, disclosed this on Friday at a press briefing in Abuja, noting that weekly cholera cases had declined substantially from the peak recorded earlier in the year.
However, Mr Idris said the decline in cases should not be interpreted as the end of the outbreak.
“The encouraging news is that weekly cases have declined substantially from the peak recorded earlier in the season. The proportion of reported cases resulting in death is also considerably lower than it was at the same time last year,” he said.
“This is important progress. But I want to be very clear: the outbreak is not over.
Cholera transmission
Mr Idris said the country is still in the rainy season, when cholera transmission can increase because flooding may contaminate water sources and overwhelm sanitation systems.
He said one of the clearest lessons from the outbreak is the importance of early access to treatment, noting that people who seek care early have better outcomes.
“In Borno State, where the majority of this year’s cases have occurred, outcomes have been better where treatment has been brought closer to affected communities,” he said.
However, he said treatment alone could not end the outbreak. “But the data are telling us something equally important: while treatment saves lives, we cannot treat our way out of cholera.”
According to the NCDC boss, unsafe water, open defecation, damaged water distribution systems, poor hygiene infrastructure, and inadequate sanitation in schools, markets, and other public institutions remain among the underlying problems driving transmission.
He called on state and local governments to improve access to safe water and sanitation, strengthen water-quality monitoring, repair critical water infrastructure and address open defecation.
He also urged authorities to ensure that high-risk local government areas have functional treatment and rapid-response capacity.
Diphtheria
Mr Idris also disclosed that Nigeria has recorded more than 10,000 confirmed cases of diphtheria this year.
He said while the disease remains a substantial burden, the proportion of confirmed cases resulting in death has declined considerably compared with the same period last year.
He said most confirmed cases are concentrated in a few states, particularly Kano, Borno and Bauchi.
“The central issue is that too many children remain unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated,” Mr Idris said.
ALSO READ: Cholera outbreak in Borno overwhelms health facilities as suspected cases exceed 35,000
He identified vaccine hesitancy, insecurity, hard-to-reach communities, displacement, and population movement as factors that make it difficult to reach every child who needs protection.
He stressed that diphtheria is vaccine-preventable and called for improved vaccination coverage, particularly in affected, underserved and hard-to-reach communities.
NCDC response
The NCDC said it was coordinating the public health response to both outbreaks with state governments and partners, including strengthening surveillance and laboratory capacity, supporting healthcare workers and deploying National Rapid Response Teams to affected states.
For cholera, the response includes oral cholera vaccination in high-burden areas, water chlorination, rehabilitation of water sources and hygiene promotion.
The agency said its teams had investigated transmission sources and assessed water supply points in Borno, while in Bauchi, oral rehydration points had been established, treatment capacity strengthened, and active case search intensified.
For diphtheria, the response is focused on strengthening vaccination coverage and rapidly identifying and managing cases. Reactive vaccination is also being conducted in affected areas.

items.title: Police probe death of bolt driver found with chest injury
items.summary: Police said the circumstances surrounding the death remain unclear. The post Police probe death of bolt driver found with chest injury appeared first on Premium Times Nigeria.
items.body_text:
The police in Cross River State have commenced an investigation into the death of a 29-year-old man, Emmanuel Ita, whose body was discovered in connection with a Honda City vehicle along the Target–Udy King axis of Calabar on Friday.
Mr Ita, a resident of Ikot Effanga Mkpa, Calabar, was found dead after an incident whose circumstances remain unclear, according to a statement issued by the police spokesperson, Sunday Eitokpah.
The police said officials were immediately deployed to the scene after receiving information about the incident.
However, the deceased’s remains had already been taken by his family to a hospital mortuary, where a preliminary examination revealed an injury on his chest.
Investigation begins
The police said it has commenced a preliminary investigation to establish the circumstances surrounding Mr Ita’s death.
“His vehicle has been recovered, while relevant evidence is being preserved for further forensic and investigative examination,” Mr Eitokpah said.
The police urged members of the public to refrain from drawing conclusions or circulating unverified information, saying the circumstances surrounding the death had not been established.
“The command urges members of the public to refrain from drawing conclusions or circulating unverified information, as the circumstances of the incident have not yet been conclusively established,” the statement said.
The case, according to the command, will be transferred to the State Criminal Investigation Department (SCID) for “discreet and comprehensive investigation.”
The police said any significant development would be communicated to the public.
“The command remains committed to uncovering the facts and ensuring that anyone found responsible is brought to justice,” Mr Eitokpah said.
Earlier report alleged stabbing
The police statement followed an earlier report by an online newspaper which alleged that a bolt driver was stabbed to death by three unidentified robbers along Target Road in Calabar South.
The report said the driver had picked up three men along Mbukpa Road and was heading towards Calabar Municipality when the passengers allegedly ordered him to stop and surrender his car key.
According to the report, the driver resisted and was allegedly stabbed while driving. He reportedly managed to reach a nearby filling station before losing control of the vehicle, which veered into a gutter and struck a pavement.
The report said the three suspects fled, while passersby took the injured driver to the General Hospital, Calabar, where he was confirmed dead.
The police, however, did not confirm the robbery or stabbing allegation in their statement. It said only a preliminary examination revealed an injury on Mr Ita’s chest.
Similar killing in Bayelsa
The incident occurred over a year after the killing of another Bolt driver in Bayelsa State, reported by PREMIUM TIMES in May 2025.
The driver was found shot dead inside his vehicle at Samphino Road Junction in Yenagoa. Police evacuated his remains and deposited them at a mortuary for autopsy.
Residents suspected robbery, while police investigated the circumstances and sought trip data from Bolt to help identify possible perpetrators.
In the Calabar case, the police said their investigation would establish what happened and determine whether anyone was responsible.

items.title: Fake Agency Scandal: Tinubu orders forensic audit of IPPIS, MDAs
items.summary: President Tinubu’s directive follows the Federal Executive Council's resolution on 19 August 2026, in response to findings by the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) on “fake agencies”, ghost workers, and other control failures. The post Fake Agency Scandal: Tinubu orders forensic audit of IPPIS, MDAs appeared first on Premium Times Nigeria.
items.body_text:
President Bola Tinubu has directed the Minister of Finance and Co-ordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, to oversee and coordinate a comprehensive forensic audit of federal government systems.
The audit will include a review of the Integrated Personnel and Payroll Information System (IPPIS), federal government agencies, and their administration and internal controls.
President Tinubu’s directive follows the Federal Executive Council’s resolution on 19 August 2026, in response to findings by the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) on “fake agencies”, ghost workers, and other control failures.
The exercise will establish the nature and extent of weaknesses in government’s control system, and determine how such weaknesses have been exploited.
The review will comprise two interconnected components.
The first will focus on a forensic audit of government systems, particularly IPPIS and related payroll, personnel, pension and financial-management platforms. It will examine reported cases of ghost workers and payroll fraud, reconcile the figures identified by the ICPC, trace how fictitious or ineligible persons were enrolled, and review access, identity, biometric and bank-account controls.
The exercise will also examine the interfaces between IPPIS and other government platforms, including GIFMIS, Remita, the Treasury Single Account (TSA) and Sub-TSA, to determine whether fraud resulted from system defects, process failures, inadequate segregation of duties or deliberate circumvention.
The second component of the audit will cover all federal government agencies, departments, commissions, councils, parastatals and other government bodies. It will establish a definitive inventory of such bodies and verify their legal basis, while examining how entities obtain official recognition, budgetary consideration, correspondence privileges, office facilities and access to government systems.
The exercise will assess governance, procurement, internal-audit, and oversight controls across Government to close systemic weaknesses that could allow irregular entities or persons to access public resources.
President Tinubu directed that the exercise be conducted with the highest standards of independence, professionalism and forensic integrity.
ALSO READ: PFIPC Probe: ICPC submits interim report to Tinubu, uncovers two more fake agencies
The audit team will have access to relevant government systems and records. It will collaborate with the ICPC to ensure that the review complements all ongoing investigations, prosecutions and recoveries.
President Tinubu expects the exercise to go beyond identifying individual cases of fraud or administrative failure by strengthening the architecture of Government, closing systemic loopholes, improving data verification and reconciliation, reinforcing accountability, and ensuring that only duly constituted entities and eligible personnel have access to Government resources.
The exercise underscores the President’s commitment to strengthening transparency, accountability, fiscal governance and institutional integrity across the federal government.
Bayo Onanuga
Special Adviser to the President

items.title: World's youngest reigning traditional monarch dies aged 34
items.summary: King Oyo ascended to the throne of Uganda's Tooro kingdom when he was just three years old.
items.body_text:
World's youngest reigning traditional monarch dies aged 34
- Published
A traditional Ugandan ruler named as the world's youngest monarch has died aged 34, his prime minster announced.
Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV became king of Tooro in western Uganda at just three years old in 1995 after the death of his father.
The Tooro kingdom did not disclose the cause of King Oyo's death, but a Ugandan government minister was quoted in local media saying that he had been critically ill and was seeking treatment in the US.
Though Uganda is governed by an elected president and parliament, it has several traditional kingdoms which continue to have significant cultural influence despite not having political power.
Oyo, who Guinness World Records listed as the world's youngest reigning monarch, external, ruled over more than two million people. He was the 13th monarch of a kingdom that was founded in the early 19th Century.
Announcing his death, Tooro's Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki called his passing on Thursday an "immeasurable loss" to the royal family and the people of Tooro.
"I call upon all the people of Tooro to remain united, calm and prayerful during this profoundly difficult time," Akiiki said on Friday. "May His Majesty the King rest in eternal peace."
The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch.
Oyo was not officially married, but Akiiki said "the continuity of the Crown is assured".
"His Majesty leaves behind a Prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro Kingdom," he explained.
When he became king in 1995 a regency, which included the queen mother, was established until Oyo turned 18 when there was an official coronation.
The young king was well respected by his people and according to a report in the Daily Monitor newspaper he promoted causes such as youth empowerment, education and climate conservation, as well as HIV/Aids awareness.
The country's largest and most influential traditional institution, the Buganda Kingdom, said it mourned with the people of Tooro following the death of their monarch, labelling him a valuable figure to Uganda.
Similarly, the Rwenzururu Kingdom also extended its condolences to "all those mourning this great loss", according to local media reports.
Others have also paid their respects to the late king.
The Federation of Uganda Football Associations, honoured King Oyo as a "true friend of the beautiful game", and announced a moment of silence before the kick-off of all matches until 4 September in memory of his "legacy, love, passion and contribution" to the sport.
Government minister Margaret Muhanga described the mood in the kingdom as "sombre... you can't see anyone smiling".
The king was "at the prime of his life", she said in a video shared on social media, "as young as he was, he had an impact on his kingdom".
Muhanga said they would be planting a million trees in his honour during the mourning period, and wants to ask the neighbouring districts in Tooro to do the same.
Uganadan musician Juliana Kanyomozi called it a "very dark day for Tooro", in an Instagram post. "Gone too soon. What a loss!!!!"
Meanwhile, pop star-turned-politician Bobi Wine, called for King Oyo's "soul to rest in eternal peace".

items.title: Two-year curfew lifted in Sudan's capital
items.summary: The military authorities retook control of the city 18 months ago, but the conflict continues elsewhere.
items.body_text:
Two-year curfew lifted in Sudan's capital
- Published
Sudan's military-led government has lifted a curfew and state of emergency in Khartoum imposed more than two years ago, state media says.
The authorities are taking this step 18 months after the army seized back control of the capital from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which it has been fighting in a civil war now in its fourth year.
But clashes continue in the south and west, with mounting evidence that the war is spilling across Sudan's borders.
More than two million of the roughly five million people who fled Khartoum after war erupted in April 2023 have returned to the city since fighting there ended in March 2025, according to the International Organization for Migration.
The aim of lifting the curfew is to help restore normal life to the capital.
The government has reopened the city's main airport for some flights and is encouraging businesses and embassies to come back.
But residents still struggle to rebuild their livelihoods.
Many have found widespread damage with many buildings looted. And they have to cope with constant power blackouts, due to alleged RSF drone attacks on electricity infrastructure and a lack of government funds to carry out repairs.
"The targeting of the electricity sector in particular was very significant," a spokesperson for the Khartoum state government, Altayeb Saadeldin, told the Reuters news agency, listing looting of copper wires and fuel and other components, as well as drone attacks, as reasons for the outages.
An RSF source responded that the allegations were "incorrect and army propaganda".
- Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity 
  - Published7 August
Despite lifting the state of emergency, the authorities remain wary of RSF infiltration. The Sudan News Agency said security patrols would continue operating across the state and locals traveling at night would need to carry identification documents.
Reports compiled by BBC Monitoring say the army continues to carry out security sweeps across greater Khartoum, targeting alleged RSF sleeper cells, undocumented foreigners and criminals involved in illegal activities.
In the meantime, there is growing concern that the war is drawing in neighbouring countries.
Chad is accusing the Sudanese army of carrying out an air strike that hit a military convoy in Ennedi-Est province, about 100km (62 miles) inside Chadian territory, on 20 August. It has reportedly put its forces along the border on maximum alert.
Sudan has rejected the charge, saying it is surprised that its army was blamed without an independent investigation.
In a statement, the foreign ministry said it "affirms that the Sudanese army fulfils its constitutional duty to defend Sudan's sovereignty, security and territorial integrity, and to confront the threats facing the country, while remaining committed to respecting the sovereignty of neighbouring states and refraining from targeting their territories".
Sudan accuses Chad of permitting the passage of RSF military supplies delivered by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) through its airports and border crossings.
The UAE and Chad deny the allegations despite similar findings by UN experts and investigative reports by international media.
The attack on the Chadian convoy prompted the US Senior Adviser for Arab and African Affairs, Massad Boulos to express "deep concern" about the risk of Sudan's war threatening regional peace and stability.
Boulos has been urging the parties to immediately accept a humanitarian truce. He has grown increasingly frustrated with the Sudanese military, which refuses to engage in a peace process unless the RSF disarms and withdraws from the territory it has occupied.
"The United States condemns the SAF's recent air strikes inside Chad," Boulos wrote in a post on X. "There is no military solution to this conflict - and absolutely no justification for expanding the violence beyond Sudan's borders.

items.title: Dutch court sentences man to life over Rwanda genocide
items.summary: The court in The Hague convicted the 66-year-old of war crimes and the crime of genocide.
items.body_text:
Dutch court sentences man to life over Rwanda genocide
- Published
A court in the Netherlands has sentenced a Dutch-Rwandan man to life for his involvement in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.
The 66-year-old, named only as Eugene N, was accused, among other things, of throwing a hand grenade into a crowd of Tutsis who were seeking shelter in a stadium. He was convicted of war crimes and the crime of genocide, having acted with "genocidal intent", the judge said.
Rwanda had sought his extradition in 2014 but the authorities in the Netherlands then launched their own investigation into N, who had become a Dutch citizen.
In 100 days in April 1994, an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus people were killed by Hutu extremists.
The court in The Hague heard N held an authoritative position in the community at the time of the massacre, overseeing around 1,000 people in Mbazi in southern Rwanda.
"The suspect was a man who was held in high regard and must have been aware of his role and the influence he had as a local administrator," the court explained, adding that he "committed multiple severe crimes".
At a football stadium, he instructed Hutus not to let any of the Tutsis escape. Trapped inside, they were pelted with stones, shot at and had hand grenades thrown at them.
Any who had survived, were killed with clubs and machetes, the court said.
Prior to the stadium massacre, N had watched on as people looted houses and set them on fire.
"Only a lifelong prison sentence does justice to the immense suffering that has been inflicted on the victims and the bereaved families," the court said.
As part of the Dutch investigation opened in 2020, more than 30 witnesses were interviewed. N was subsequently arrested in 2024.
N denied all the charges, the AFP news agency reports, alleging that he was a victim who had lost family in "those horrific events".
"The case has torn his scars open again. He is a broken man," his lawyers are quoted as saying by AFP. They had moved to seek acquittals on all accounts. N was acquitted of the incitement to genocide.
His defence team said they will "almost certainly appeal the charges", according to local news agency ANP.

Jared Kushner Is the Face of American Oligarchy
Trump’s son-in-law embodies the rise of a trend that threatens to ignite a new nuclear age.
On Nov. 16, 2025, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky listened on speakerphone to an unfamiliar voice. This new interlocutor, speaking with a reedy U.S. accent, had a plan for Zelensky: a series of bullet points, all approved by the U.S. president, for what Zelensky would have to do to end Ukraine’s war with Russia.
The list of demands ran on and on. There were new limits Ukraine would have to place on its military, preventing Ukraine from ever matching Russia’s battlefield advantages. There was the reality that Ukraine would have to give up any dreams of ever joining NATO. There were the revelations that, even as Ukraine’s ability to defend itself shrank, Russia would see sanctions soon lifted, and that Moscow would once more be welcomed into the geopolitical fold, as if the war had never happened.

There was the reality that Ukraine would have to give up any dreams of ever joining NATO. There were the revelations that, even as Ukraine’s ability to defend itself shrank, Russia would see sanctions soon lifted, and that Moscow would once more be welcomed into the geopolitical fold, as if the war had never happened.
But that wasn’t all. As this new voice instructed Zelensky, Ukraine would have to finally, formally give up not just Crimea, but all of the Donbas—including territory that Russia hadn’t even occupied. After years of fighting, and after millions of casualties, Ukraine would have to cede territory—and abandon Ukrainian populations—that Russia never conquered.
The proposals were beyond anything Zelensky or his administration had ever heard. They went beyond anything anyone outside Moscow had ever proposed. The demands effectively gelded Ukraine, ensuring that Kyiv would remain forever prone to Russia. Indeed, they read less as a list of negotiated points, and more as a wish list of outcomes straight from the Kremlin.
Which is exactly what they were. Zelensky didn’t know it at the time, but the list of demands had originated not in any Western capital, but in Moscow. And the man unspooling these new demands—Jared Kushner, now emerging from the shadows, taking center stage in the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine—was there to tell Zelensky that the plan was now Washington’s, and that Kushner was there to make sure the plan was now implemented.
The entire sordid saga of Kushner’s supposed “peace plan” in late 2025 generated immediate headlines and swift backlash. But while many focused on the bungled, haphazard nature of the plan itself—and on how little anyone outside of Kushner and his partner, Steve Witkoff, actually knew about the details ahead of time—there was less attention on the implications of the proposal, or what it meant for the oligarchic takeover of U.S. foreign policy. items.title: Getting Confucius Wrong
items.summary: A new translation of a key Chinese text is dangerously lacking in expertise.
items.body_text:
Getting Confucius Wrong
A new translation of a key Chinese text is dangerously lacking in expertise.
Save for Mao Zedong, there may be no more famous Chinese figures than Confucius, who is believed to have lived from 551 to 479 B.C. Acclaim started early: Soon after Confucius’ death, all sorts of sayings were attributed to him, often collected in writing. Of these collections, the Analects became the most important, emerging between the 2nd and 1st century B.C.
Confucius and the Analects became foundational aspects of Chinese culture, and one of the main lenses through which to understand China. Since the 1930s, Confucius has stood next to Moses on the east pediment of the U.S. Supreme Court Building. There are now so many translations of the Analects into English alone that it has been possible to compare them through natural language processing models. Chinese President Xi Jinping and other leaders often promote the Analects, and the People’s Republic of China promotes its own worldwide Confucius Institutes for studying Chinese culture –even though it viciously attacked Confucianism for three decades after its foundation.

The Analects: A Contemporary Translation by Erin Cline, a professor at Georgetown University, is a new translation that aims, in Cline’s account, to counter inaccuracies in how the text has traditionally been read in its depictions of women. This follows her 2022 book, The Analects: A Guide, in which she corrects what she considers another problem: the lack of discussions of the Analects as a “sacred” text.
Unfortunately, both works fail to acknowledge centuries of studies that have already extensively covered these issues.
Take Analects 8.20, a passage central to Cline’s argument that the Analects is not misogynistic. Analects 8.20 references King Wu, the founder of the Zhou dynasty who was celebrated as a model ruler. Wu played a crucial role in overthrowing the previous Shang dynasty, which was also known as the Yin dynasty.
As it’s written, Analects 8.20 includes the sentence “There is a woman among [King Wu’s ministers], nine persons, and that is it.” A previous passage refers to Wu having ten advisors. It is just as confusing in Chinese as in English, and many interpretations supposed some text was missing. Cline takes it to show that, “[c]ontrary to what some commentators and contemporary translations have suggested, there is nothing in the original to suggest misogyny.”
To Cline, the sentence suggests simple acknowledgement of a female advisor. Test yourself on the week of Aug. 22: A U.N. monitoring mission goes to Congo, the U.S. unveils an economic plan against Iran, and Putin issues a warning.
U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” this week. Beyond that eye-popping story, what else happened? Find out with our international news quiz!

1. In a video released on Sunday, Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella announced he would order the country’s immigration service to begin doing what?
Recent government data suggests that there are hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans who have fled economic and political crises to Colombia—and now they have to worry about deportation, FP’s Catherine Osborn writes in Latin America Brief.
2. A United Nations-backed monitoring mission deployed to the Democratic Republic of the Congo on Monday. What is it meant to oversee?
The peace deal brokered by Trump in eastern Congo to disarm M23 means nothing to locals—and many would prefer M23 remains, Krista Karch and Merveille Kavira Luneghe reported in January.
3. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday unveiled a plan to cut Iran off from the global economy. What is that campaign called?
If policymakers work on the assumption that the worst of the economic fallout from the Iran war is behind us, that could lead to true economic catastrophe, FP’s Emma Ashford and Matthew Rojansky argue.
4. What did Russian President Vladimir Putin say on Monday would happen to privately owned critical infrastructure facilities if their owners failed to protect them from Ukrainian attacks—or repair them after strikes?
Concerns of nuclear escalation if Russia were on the verge of losing in Ukraine are misplaced. Other great powers have previously been humbled in conflict without resorting to nuclear warfare, Andreas Umland argues.
5. The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces on Tuesday announced the official dissolution of the group. What will now happen to its remaining fighters?
The practical and symbolic nature of daily governance in the Kurdish-led northeastern territory, formerly known as Rojava, remains fraught as it integrates into Syria, Hanna Davis reported earlier this month.
6. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that CIA director John Ratcliffe traveled to Russia earlier this week to do what?
The trip came after new U.S. intelligence assessments suggested that Putin could seek to launch a limited attack on a member of the trans-Atlantic alliance, FP’s John Haltiwanger and Rishi Iyengar write in Situation Report.
7. Zambian police said on Thursday that opposition leader Brian Mundubile and his running mate are in police custody after being questioned in connection with which alleged crime?
The results of the presidential election earlier this month are still being contested amid allegations of interference by incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema, FP’s Nosmot Gbadamosi reports in Africa Brief.

Taiwanese Defense Minister Wellington Koo criticized the opposition’s plan as limiting Taipei’s ability to bolster its drone capabilities, FP’s Alexandra Sharp reports in World Brief.

The robot beat Bolt’s record by 0.19 seconds, slamming full speed into a padded wall and crashing to the ground to end its race, the New York Times reports.

items.title: A Great Rebalancing Is Coming
items.summary: Who will bear the costs of a global trade adjustment?
items.body_text:
The trade imbalances that have come to characterize the global economy are fundamentally untenable. China, Germany, and a handful of other economies run large, persistent trade surpluses, while the United States absorbs much of these surpluses by running the world’s largest trade deficit. Sooner or later, something must give. For an advanced, capital-rich economy such as that of the United States, an enduring trade deficit will bring with it either rising unemployment or rising debt, neither of which is sustainable.
In theory, the major surplus and deficit economies could agree on a coordinated adjustment in which surplus countries would expand domestic demand and deficit countries would gradually reduce their dependence on debt-fueled consumption, allowing the imbalances to shrink without a sharp contraction in global demand. That would be the sensible solution.
But because the major players disagree about the causes of the imbalances, they are unlikely to come to such a solution. China attributes them to excessive U.S. consumption and fiscal deficits; the United States blames foreign industrial, trade, and currency policies; and Europe has yet to settle on a coherent diagnosis. As a result, they all have proposed remedies that are at odds with one another. Beijing wants deficit countries to save more and prefers not to change China’s growth model. Washington wants surplus countries to reduce their surpluses by redistributing income to the household sector. European leaders continue to advocate for multilateral cooperation and rules-based trade. This makes the chances of a coordinated response slim. And as the economic analyst Martin Wolf wrote in the Financial Times earlier this year, if there is little prospect of preemptive action, “the second-best option is to prepare for a crisis.”
Individual economies are now doing just that. History shows that trade imbalances of this scale almost always end painfully—and that the pain of the adjustment is not distributed evenly. High levels of debt combined with low productivity makes a country more likely to bear the burden of a trade adjustment, but economic and political power can also give it the tools to pass the burden off to others. Among the three main economic players today, China is the most vulnerable, the United States has the most capacity to reduce its exposure, and Europe possesses latent power but a dubious ability to use it. None of their maneuvers to protect themselves are likely to reduce the risk or overall cost of a crisis. The question is only who will feel the brunt of the losses when it arrives.
HISTORY REPEATS ITSELF
Large, persistent trade imbalances have cropped up periodically over the past century, and they are rarely benign. One such episode occurred during the 1920s, when a surge in American productivity was not accompanied by rising wages. Production soared past consumption, and the United States ran enormous trade surpluses. Europe ran the corresponding deficits, as many countries borrowed heavily abroad to rebuild economies devastated by war. Germany in particular borrowed extensively to finance both domestic growth and its reparations payments. American domestic debt also rose rapidly, much of it to fund consumption and asset speculation.
As the imbalances persisted and U.S. manufacturing expanded at the expense of European manufacturing, protectionist pressures intensified. France devalued its currency in 1927, the United Kingdom abandoned the gold standard in 1931, and the same year Germany imposed import restrictions and rationed access to foreign currency. Even the United States, whose manufacturers and farmers complained that weak demand was threatening domestic production and employment, passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act in 1930.

items.title: Leave Europe to the Europeans
items.summary: The case for a U.S. military drawdown.
items.body_text:
In a 1987 New York Times advertisement, long before he became president, Donald Trump insisted that “America should stop paying to defend countries that can afford to defend themselves.” This has been a consistent theme of his foreign policy rhetoric since he first moved into the White House, and he has been especially focused on applying it to Europe.
During his first term, Trump jolted European allies by threatening to withdraw the United States from NATO, arguing that its members were not spending enough on their own defense and were free-riding on American taxpayers. Ultimately, he did not make good on the threat. All his administration mustered was a late, failed effort in the summer of 2020 to remove 12,000 troops from Germany.
This time around, his administration has adopted burden shifting as a rallying cry and seems poised to act on it. Almost immediately after taking office, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth traveled to Brussels to inform his counterparts that the United States would have to focus on priorities other than Europe’s defense. Europe itself, he said, needed to “take ownership of conventional security on the continent.” Last month, to turn this vision into reality, the Pentagon launched its Europe Posture Review, which is intended to be a critical assessment of U.S. troop deployments and basing commitments on the continent. Announcing it at the NATO defense ministerial, Hegseth was clear: “Europe can and must take primary responsibility for its conventional defense.” Such an outcome would amount to a transformation in the transatlantic alliance.
Since the founding of NATO after World War II, the United States has underwritten Europe’s defense and held the top military command position in the alliance. More than 75 years later, it still accounts for about 60 percent of NATO members’ military expenditures and stations some 80,000 troops on the continent and in the United Kingdom. Decades of American dominance have left Europe reliant on U.S. leadership, technology, and spending.
If the Trump administration is serious about shifting defense responsibilities to Europe, then the posture review offers a rare opportunity. A substantial reduction in the U.S. military presence in Europe over the next two years would force the continent to build forces it has so far left to the United States, while also putting Washington on sounder defense footing. The United States is $40 trillion in debt and adding roughly $2 trillion per year, with no prospect of major fiscal reforms. Despite this dire fiscal picture, it spends about $100 billion on Europe’s defense each year.
The problem is not new. Although U.S. administrations since Dwight Eisenhower have urged Europe to do more for its own defense, Europeans have consistently shirked their obligations. Even today, some European leaders hold out hope that if they can wait out Trump’s second term, NATO will return to “normal.” Only the withdrawal of U.S. forces will convince allies that the United States truly intends to turn over responsibility for the region’s conventional defense. Nothing else will force them to plan for a future in which Washington is no longer in the lead. Such a move will draw resistance from European leaders and the U.S. Congress. But a smaller footprint is vital to relieve U.S. overextension, and it can be done without harming American interests.
A TEMPORARY SHIELD
The presence of U.S. military personnel in Europe in the late 1940s and early 1950s was supposed to be a temporary shield as Western European states rebuilt economies devastated by war. But the troops stayed long after that rebuilding was complete. At the height of the Cold War, the United States had more than 400,000 troops on the continent. When the Soviet Union collapsed, NATO lost its formal justification.

items.title: India Is Sticking With America—for Now
items.summary: But Trump’s coercion could force Modi’s Hand.
items.body_text:
President Donald Trump, in his second term, has severely tested the U.S.-Indian relationship. He has slapped tariffs on India, threatened to impose secondary sanctions, gotten considerably closer to Pakistan, and enthusiastically engaged with China—the country India considers its biggest long-term military threat. Yet these strains have not led to the rupture that some observers had predicted. Nor have they forced a fundamental reorientation of Indian foreign policy. Instead, New Delhi has adopted what might be called an “America plus” strategy, in which it seeks to sustain partnership with the United States while widening its engagement with other powers, namely U.S. allies.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has responded with unusual restraint to Trump’s provocations and has resisted demands to pull away from Washington. With the United States, India has continued trade negotiations, increased defense cooperation, and expanded technological and commercial ties. In addition, he has sustained the Quad, a regional security organization that also includes Australia, Japan, and the United States; drawn closer to U.S. allies; preserved relations with Russia; and sought to lower tensions with China. These efforts do not represent a retreat from the United States or a strategy of multialignment. India is trying to reduce its exposure to American volatility, but it still recognizes that Washington is its most important partner.
After all, when it comes to cultivating a great-power patron, India doesn’t have better options. China and Russia will never buy Indian goods and services on the scale that the United States does, nor can Russia help India balance China. These realities have protected the U.S.-Indian relationship so far. But if Trump continues to bully India, public opinion could force Modi to abandon his restrained approach.
GROWING APART?
Through 2024, Modi and his ruling Bharatiya Janata Party were excited at the prospect of Trump’s return to power. Modi had established an unusually warm personal relationship with the president during the latter’s first term. In 2019 and 2020, they headlined rallies together in Houston and Ahmadabad, expanded bilateral cooperation on defense, and developed a common approach to Asian security.
At the start of Trump’s second term, it seemed the friendly personal relationship between the two leaders would continue. At a White House meeting in February 2025, they announced an ambitious agenda for trade, defense, energy, and technology. To signal goodwill, the Indian prime minister accommodated Trump by slashing some of India’s tariffs on U.S. products and accepting a planeload of deported immigrants.
But the relationship soon soured. Trump took credit in May 2025 for ending a brief military conflict between India and Pakistan. While the Pakistanis hailed Trump’s intervention, the Indians refused to acknowledge that the president had done anything of the sort, sticking to New Delhi’s standard position that its disputes with Islamabad are purely bilateral and do not require outside mediation. Trump then took a shine to Pakistan’s army chief, Syed Asim Munir, and elevated Pakistan in the White House’s diplomatic priorities by using Islamabad as a mediator in negotiations with Iran and blessing the trilateral security pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey.
 Modi has largely avoided confrontations with Trump.
Trump also became friendlier with China, another Indian rival. In his first term, he sought to build stronger partnerships with Australia, India, Indonesia, and Japan to construct a new regional architecture in Asia to balance China. She and our colleagues just released a five-part podcast series called How to Touch Grass, and in this episode, Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel talks with Beck about why people are nostalgic for the pre-internet days, how our brains are changing, and the good that can come from getting lost.

They take you up and then they probe you, or they do whatever they do, and then when you come back down, you don’t know what happened. It’s erased. It’s lost time. So I feel like I have emerged from lost time and like what happened during that time is unclear, but I don’t feel good.

Over five episodes, Julie Beck and her co-host and producer, Natalie Brennan, explore what exactly is happening in this moment that has so many of us out there feeling like we need to renegotiate our relationships to our technology.
At the beginning of this year, I made a few predictions about trends that we might see, and one of them was that there would be what I was calling a scrolling backlash. That people are just really tired of their phones, of the algorithmic internet, of this idea that they’re being manipulated all the time, and that their attention is being directed towards things that don’t make them feel good or whole or happy. It’s a loss that just can’t be separated from the devices that we use.
How to Touch Grass digs into so many of the ideas that I’ve been trying to poke at here in the first year of this podcast. Our motto here at Galaxy Brain is that we pay attention to where we pay attention, which also happens to be exactly what I found so valuable about Julie and Natalie’s work. And so I decided to bring Julie on here today to talk about this moment and to talk about what she’s learned in this series. How badly have our attention spans actually been fractured? items.title: The Limits of Yayoi Kusama’s Infinity
items.summary: The visionary artist once challenged ways of seeing—until she was seen by everyone.
items.body_text:
The Limits of Yayoi Kusama’s Infinity
The visionary artist once challenged ways of seeing—until she was seen by everyone.
Years before the polka-dotted pumpkins, before the Instagrammable Infinity Mirror Rooms, Yayoi Kusama made art that was charged with oppositional energy. Her performances, in which she painted dots onto the naked bodies of her collaborators, were an expression of ’60s counterculture. They were protests against the Vietnam War, rebukes to the art market. Her Accumulations—soft sculptures of furniture or common household items covered in stuffed, handsewn penis shapes—were hilarious critiques of phallocentrism and early examples of feminist art.
Kusama was, in other words, part of the artistic avant-garde. Her death, at 97, is a cold reminder that the avant-garde no longer exists.
You could point to Andy Warhol, Jeff Koons, Takashi Murakami, or Keith Haring, but in many ways, no one epitomizes the collapse of the avant-garde more vividly than Kusama. I’m mostly a fan of her work. It’s very hard not to like her Infinity Mirror Room installations and playful gourds, and not to smile when you see Kusama’s endearing face framed by her signature brightly colored bobbed wig. But at a certain point, you can’t help but feel that she stopped being an artist and chose instead to become a highly profitable brand.
In death as in life, her name bestrides a tightly managed, commercially successful global enterprise with diverse revenue streams, including high-profile partnerships with luxury labels, licensed merchandise, and strictly managed intellectual-property protection. Kusama’s large-scale sculptures and immersive installations break attendance records at museums and galleries around the world, and her works regularly set records at auction. In her final years, she was one of the world’s top-selling contemporary artists.
Decades before all of that, though, Kusama was a creative maverick. After moving to New York from Tokyo in the late 1950s, she became a pioneer of both pop art and minimalism, then a key figure in performance art. She called her early breakthrough paintings—expansive, swirling fields of tightly packed dots—Infinity Nets. Before even Andy Warhol (although after Marcel Duchamp), she made her own persona an expression of her art, paving the way for such figures as Gilbert and George, the British-artist duo who made life itself a performance.
Kusama’s artworks had countercultural energy. They fought against cliché. They critiqued patriarchy. They broke down starchy inhibitions and wobbled magnificently on the edge of the rational. They tried, in other words, to open up new ways of seeing.
That was what the avant-garde was all about: It was an attempt to see the world afresh. For many of its leading figures, from the Impressionists in the 1870s to conceptual artists a century later, this also meant proposing new and better solutions to the problem of how to be and how to live together. These proposals, many times rooted in sympathy and love, were presented as alternatives to the political structures and market logic that had so often led to war, exploitation, hopelessness, and suffering.
Even when attempts to turn these imagined alternatives into reality failed—and often dismally—the avant-garde stood in a clear relationship to modernity’s traumas. It was like the whistle cap in the spout of a boiling kettle: both a release of suppressed pressures (psychic and cultural) and an alarm.
But society got sick of hearing the alarm. And the kettle got tired of whistling.
Kusama, having experienced a period of art-world success, had her own breakdown after returning to Tokyo permanently in 1973. Two years later, she checked herself in to a psychiatric institution, where she became a permanent resident from 1977 until her death. The institution was within walking distance of her multistory studio.

items.title: What Dolly Parton Knew About Reading
items.summary: She wanted to be remembered, most of all, as the “book lady.”
items.body_text:
What Dolly Parton Knew About Reading
She wanted to be remembered, most of all, as the “book lady.”
This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here.
My best friend’s baby got mail from Dolly Parton on the day the singer died. This wasn’t unexpected: He’s been receiving books from Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library for all 10 months of his life. (This month’s selection was Bedtime, Here I Come, by D. J. Steinberg.) And he wasn’t alone—the Imagination Library sends free books to children every month from birth to age 5; the program has passed out more than 300 million books in five countries. My colleague Annie Joy Williams wrote earlier this week about the legacy of Parton—and her books program—in Tennessee, the home state that all three of us share. But the Imagination Library has expanded far beyond that territory. When I lived in an apartment building in Washington, D.C., I would see books bearing the library’s distinctive seal on a table in the lobby—volumes too big for my neighbor’s mailbox, quietly awaiting little hands.
First, here are three new stories from The Atlantic’s Books section:
Stories about Parton’s generosity are spreading widely: She helped fund a COVID-19 vaccine and filmed herself getting the shot when many Americans were hesitant. She opened a sanctuary for bald eagles! She did so many things for so many kinds of Americans, and especially Tennesseans, that I find it hard to keep track. But she said, many times, that she’d be happy to be remembered not as a generational talent or a dolled-up diva but as “the book lady.” Parton grew up in poverty in East Tennessee, and she frequently cited her illiterate father as the inspiration for her books program, which she founded in 1995. I don’t know whether all of Parton’s fans knew how high she ranked literacy on her list of important causes, but when I watched tributes to Parton roll in this week, I noted that people I’d grown up with in Tennessee (mostly young women like me) kept posting the same tableaus on Instagram: photos of babies and kids sitting with their parents, reading a book they’d gotten from the Imagination Library.
The photos are cute—but they also reflect something deeply important. A few years ago, I edited an essay by the children’s-book author Katherine Marsh that identified one reason young kids were less motivated to read: Schools often push them toward a “hyperfocus on analysis” and give precedence to individual paragraphs and sentences rather than entire narratives. But, Marsh argues, “the best way to present an abstract idea to kids is by hooking them on a story.” And a great way to get a kid interested in a story is by reading it aloud to them. In another article, published a year ago, Ilana Kurshan wrote about this declining but important practice, and about doing it with her son: “The delight of reading to him lay not in the pages we turned,” she wrote, “but in the wheels that seemed to turn in his mind as we read together.”
Thanks to my friends’ beloved babies and the perks of my job—which have included putting together a list of essential children’s books—I’ve been thinking a lot about the importance of reading with children. They still encounter books in schools and libraries, but Parton’s program emphasized building a bookshelf at home, where caregivers and kids can share stories as part of a daily routine. Reading aloud offers a child more than the chance to develop literacy skills. It gave Kurshan, for example, “a way to guide them as they started to understand the world, and as I started to understand them.” So, like Parton, I’ll be happy if kids see me as a “book lady.” Last week, I bought a picture book about berries for a different toddler. And although my friend’s 10-month-old already has plenty at home, I couldn’t resist mailing him a few more books.

items.title: Could Data Centers Swing an Election in Wisconsin?
items.summary: As A.I. becomes increasingly unpopular among voters, the politics of data centers are scrambling political lines across the country—including in a tight race for the Wisconsin governor’s mansion.
items.body_text:
In early March, Philip Gorman, a county supervisor in southern Wisconsin, came across a local news report that had uncovered permits related to plans for a company linked to Meta to build a hyper-scale A.I. data center in his district. The proposed data center, named Cornmaze, would cover more than four hundred acres of an aging quarry, straddling two tiny towns in Rock County, which borders Illinois. Soon, Gorman discovered that town officials and the county administrator, who was supposed to report to elected officials like him, had signed nondisclosure agreements with the developer a year earlier. Gorman told me that, when he approached the administrator, he responded by saying, “I’m not sure if I even should have told you I signed the N.D.A.”
Gorman, who has been on the Rock County Board of Supervisors since 2024, began organizing with citizens across the county who feared that the project would raise utility bills, diminish air quality, and drain the county’s groundwater, joining a growing nationwide backlash against data centers. But, while travelling around his district, he noticed that the reasons people had for opposing the project went beyond typical NIMBYism. “I’ve never seen engagement like this on any normal development issue,” Gorman said. “People don’t like that they didn’t have a vote on whether social media could take over our society. And now people see A.I. getting ready to take things over and potentially upset lives, upset society, upset jobs, and they want the ability to have a say in that.” Local residents helped set up informal community meetings to discuss the data center at the public library, and opposition kept building. Dozens of meetings followed, sometimes three a week. Meanwhile, Gorman was running for reëlection, and, in April, he won his race handily. “I won very conservative parts of the town of Beloit that I had previously lost, purely on the data-center issue,” he told me. “You can knock seven doors and hear seven different reasons why people don’t want this.”
A recent Gallup poll found that more than seventy per cent of Americans oppose data centers in their area. And, during the past several weeks, data centers have become increasingly toxic in midterm elections across the country. Opposition has become particularly central to contests in Rust Belt states, such as Republican-trending Ohio, where anti-data-center policies have appeared to boost the campaigns of the Democrats Amy Acton, who is running for governor, and Sherrod Brown, who is running for Senate. Brown’s opponent is the incumbent Jon Husted, who previously, as lieutenant governor, helped usher in an explosion of data centers in the state, many of which were developed after Ohio offered them lucrative tax breaks. Brown’s ability to hammer Husted on this issue is alarming Republican operatives, who see a Husted victory as crucial to holding a majority in the Senate. This month, Axios released a private memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee warning that data centers have become an “anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.” Other politicians are distancing themselves from their previous positions, including Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, who is up for reëlection in November, and used to champion data centers. Last week, he signed an executive order that he claimed “enacted the strictest requirements IN THE NATION” for data-center permits. “We will not be bulldozed by the lawyers for these big tech companies.”
But nowhere have the politics of data centers been more strained than in the Wisconsin governor’s race. Earlier this month, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley narrowly won the Democratic nomination after one of the most chaotic and unusual primaries in the state’s history. It may or may not be true that all happy families are alike, but it’s certainly true that any married couple with a car, happy or unhappy, must at some point decide who will do the driving. For Mahmoud Khalil and his wife, Noor Abdalla, this was not a difficult decision. Khalil, who is thirty-one, spent his youth in a Palestinian refugee camp in Damascus, where he didn’t have much time for driving lessons; until recently, he was on track to become a high-level diplomat, a career that usually involves not driving but being driven. Abdalla, on the other hand, was born and raised in Flint, Michigan, and she learned to drive before she could see easily over the dashboard. (She is still short enough that this seems to require some effort, though she is now a thirty-year-old dentist who until recently had a daily commute.) In the inveterate American tradition, she treats her car as a second living room. “It’s where I’m most comfortable,” she said this past fall, giving her steering wheel an affectionate pat.
It was a Tuesday in October, just after dawn, and a pink sun was rising over the oil-distillation towers of northern New Jersey. Abdalla was making good time from Brooklyn to the federal courthouse in Philadelphia, where the couple would observe oral arguments in what Khalil dryly called “one of my cases.” He sat in the passenger seat, holding a phone in each hand: his own, from which he texted members of his sprawling pro-bono legal team, and Abdalla’s, which he used to d.j. The music, mostly old Levantine folk songs, was interrupted every now and then by a notification from a navigation app, in English: “Police ahead.”
Khalil moved to Manhattan in 2022, and he adapted quickly to American culture. (In a sense, he even came to inhabit that most American of identities: an influencer.) At Columbia, where he was a master’s student in public and international affairs, he became perhaps the most visible pro-Palestine activist. After the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, and the Israeli invasion of Gaza, there were turbulent protests at many universities, and those at Columbia were often featured on TV news. Khalil, one of the few student protesters who never wore a mask to hide his face, became a symbol of the anti-Zionist movement. President Donald Trump, a few weeks into his second term, was standing next to Elon Musk, shilling Teslas on the White House lawn, when a reporter asked about Khalil. “I think we ought to get him the hell out of the country,” Trump said. Although Khalil was a legal permanent resident, Marco Rubio, the Secretary of State, wrote a three-paragraph memo declaring him “deportable” owing to his “beliefs, statements, or associations.” Khalil was sent to an ICE detention center in rural Louisiana, where he was held for more than a hundred days, missing the birth of his son.
In Philadelphia, Abdalla parked a few blocks from the Liberty Bell, smoothed her hijab, and swapped her sneakers for high heels. Khalil made a half-hearted attempt to disguise himself, as he often does before going out in public, putting on a baseball cap emblazoned with the word “Lucky.” Every time he approached a door, he stepped aside, bowing slightly and stretching a chivalrous arm in front of him, until everyone else had gone. He passed through security and into the marble lobby of the courthouse, where the words of a renowned jurist named Learned Hand were etched on a glass panel: “If we are to keep our democracy, there must be one commandment: Thou shalt not ration justice.”
The hearing was before three federal judges, each appointed by a different President. The casting seemed almost too on the nose. The Trump appointee, a white guy with a thick beard, interrupted early and often, his eyes bulging with incredulity.
